382.s: They recall women pianists such as Mary Lou, Hazel Scott, Beryl Booker, and singer Nellie Lutcher.
382.q: Well, a couple of years ago when they had the New Year's -- I guess the Newport Jazz Festival when they had Count Basie and Cy Oliver at the Roseland Ballroom and Arnett (Cobbs) showed up and played out of this world.

382.t: Cliff as a solo pianist who disliked accompanying
382.s: He wanted recognition as a soloist; he brought friends and Fat Cat into her Town Hall concert.
382.q: Yes, of course, I feel that when someone is recognized as a solo pianist they don't necessarily want to be accompanying, taking second fiddle to some singer, you know. But we did in '67, I believe it was, we did a concert at Town

382.t: The 1944 Black & White solo piano record
382.s: Details of a Cliff solo record made July 15, 1944, and how she announced it at the House.
382.q: Yeah. This record, it's recorded July 15, 1944 and it's a Black and White label and it was probably pressed or made in the city here and there's a company, 2117 Foster Avenue, Brooklyn, New York --

382.t: Cliff Jackson's piano roll and his child prodigy flyer
382.s: She took Cliff's piano roll of 'Hock Shop Blues' to the Hall of Fame, and has a 1909 flyer from when he was a boy pianist.
382.q: Oh, yeah. But you know what, I took it down there and I put the roll on and actually you know what, you could use this to Pete's piano because you can watch the holes in the roll and watch the keys and it's a very -- of course, "Hock Shop Blues" is just another blues but I was looking at it and you…

382.t: Cliff's piano roll on 'Parlor Piano' and his 1960s album
382.s: The roll appears on albums of piano rolls, and Cliff's Harlem Banjo-era album recalls 'Hockshop Blues'.
382.q: That's right, it's on there. And Cliff made an album in the '60s, I guess called "Harlem Banjo" with Elmer Snowden. Elmer Snowden was from Washington, D.C., too.

382.t: Pittsburgh musicians: Toodle-oo and Boots Swan
382.s: She remembers boogie-woogie pianists and Boots Swan, the most popular singer, who never recorded.
382.ch: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
382.q: I remember having seen Toodle-oo around Pittsburgh working in some little club but he would be one of the musicians I met at the Crawford Grill or at the musician's club. And the other one was "Dry Bread". Yeah, I remember him. And I remember "Dry Bread". And there were other entertainers around…

382.t: Art Tatum, soloists and small-group playing
382.s: They discuss Tatum, spontaneity, and whether she'd sing with a pianist like him, recalling a Boston bill with him.
382.q: Oh, well, there are a few recordings that Art made with the rhythm section and they couldn't keep up with Art because he was so spontaneous. I mean there was no way that you could keep up with what was going on in his head. And of course that stuff was never written down. The guys get in there,…

382.s: She names Dill Jones, Marty Napoleon and the musicians who know where to fit behind her.
382.q: Yes. There are even, you know, when you get down to the nitty-gritty, there are certain accompanists that you would prefer, you know, rather than others. Although at this particular point I worked with a lot of accompanists, pianists, and right now I've got about twenty piano players that I would…

382.t: Cliff's accompanying work and 52nd Street in 1937
382.s: He accompanied early blues singers; on 52nd Street in 1937 he did not remember her.
382.q: Cliff didn't make too many records or albums, I think that there is a 78 with Cliff Jackson, an early recording in the '20s with a group, Cliff Jackson and His Krazy Kats or something like that, earlier than these selections here.

760.s: Fred Washington, now paralyzed, influenced Steve Lewis and used chords later called modern.
760.ch: New Orleans pianists and Clarence Williams
760.q: Yeah, well the piano players that I actually know, they were older than me, but the answer ones that I know who played back in Storyville during those times was Fred Washington, which was a great piano player.

760.t: Lewis Wade, Albert Cowell, Red Cayou and other New Orleans pianists
760.s: He sketches the playing of many pianists, including Sumner Rouse, a second Big Eye Louis and Newman's father.
760.ch: New Orleans pianists and Clarence Williams
760.q: The jelly roll on and we'd have to get on. Oh yeah, the jelly roll, and I couldn't hold a life for Fred Washington. Fred Washington was playing and then they had another jazz piano player that nobody, I don't mean I never read no books or nothing on him and he was absolutely good. It was a piano…

760.s: Allen asks about Alfred Wilson and Gusty O'Neal; Robichaux knew both as good pianists.
760.ch: New Orleans pianists and Clarence Williams
760.q: Oh yeah, I know who you're speaking about now. Yeah, I know him. Yeah, he was a good piano player. He was good too. He was good. Now they had several piano players that I'm not calling their name because they wasn't the real, the best. You know, I'm not calling them all, but not really the best.

760.t: Willis, Spencer Williams, Texas pianists and McNamara
760.s: A white pianist named Willis at the Shields house, Spencer Williams, Galveston pianists, and the harmonically inventive McNamara.
760.ch: New Orleans pianists and Clarence Williams
760.q: That's right. He was on that record too. That's right, Arthur Campbell. And he was a good piano player. Now these fellas would play piano during those times. They had so many of them that I could name, but they wasn't the really top piano players. Now we had another piano player play good, a white…

760.s: Game Kid played blues and rags at parties and fish fries, did not read, and composed two pieces himself.
760.ch: New Orleans pianists and Clarence Williams
760.q: Well I tell you Game Kid was a blues piano player and he played a couple of rags, you know, he played some rags too. And he was a very famous piano player uptown during the time when I was a kid, you know. And then after.

760.s: Robichaux says Tony Jackson was a wonderful pianist despite his entertainer's reputation, and Arthur Campbell good too.
760.ch: New Orleans pianists and Clarence Williams
760.q: Yeah, yeah, yeah, he was a good piano player. O'Neal was a good piano player. And also there was another piano player, oh he played nice piano too, and he was playing in the district during the time when ... Did you ever hear Tony Jackson? Oh, Tony Jackson. He was good. Yeah, I heard Tony Jackson,…

760.t: Richard M. Jones and Clarence Williams as pianists and publishers
760.s: Both wrote many tunes but he judges neither a very good pianist; he recalls Williams's music stores.
760.ch: New Orleans pianists and Clarence Williams
760.q: Oh I know it, Mione Jones, before he left here and then when I went to Chicago I met him and we used to be around Clarence Williams when Clarence Williams had the music store. I know it.

760.s: Allen asks about Desdune names tied to Jelly Roll Morton; Robichaux has found no one who remembers Mamie.
760.ch: New Orleans pianists and Clarence Williams
760.q: I tell you, I've been trying to find out, I've been asking different fellows, these old fellows about this Mamie Desdune since I got this book of Jelly Rolls, you know. And I was reading about it and I've been asking fellows about it and it seems like they don't recall her, you know, fellows who…

259.t: Piano players: Tony Jackson, Roscoe Williams, Fats Pichon
259.s: He names good pianists, Tony Jackson's songs, blues pianist Roscoe Williams, and Walter 'Fats' Pichon.
259.q: So who were some of the good piano players you know then? Let me see. Steve Lewis? You got the right one all right. Odell, I think. Odell. Odell. Odell. Odell. Odell Wilson.

259.t: Special numbers of Big Kato, Louis Robinson and Sonny Swan
259.s: Vincent says Little Kato had funny pieces, Louis Robinson just played softly, and Sonny Swan played blues, in what was then called ragtime rather than jazz.
259.q: Yeah, Big Kato. He said, did Big Kato have any special numbers himself? Who? Big Kato. Kato. Uh, he used to come out some of the, you know, Little Kato, not Big Kato. Oh, Little Kato had. He used to come out some of the funny pieces, but I don't know where the, where the man, he's called the name,…

259.t: Blind Charlie and Steve Lewis, piano players
259.s: He recalls Blanc Charlie playing blues piano, bass and banjo, and Steve Lewis as the best floor-show pianist who needed to learn music, with some remarks on pay.
259.q: Blanc Charlie was a good blue piano too. He played piano, bass, and banditore, Blanc Charlie. Banditore too. He was just a blue playing piano, you know. He could make out his band, put a fuzz, and be a blind man, you know.

259.s: Allen and Vincent try to identify Sammy Dukie, a blind player who worked with a chambon player.
259.q: kind of nuts, I forget his name, chambon player. But we always played together then. Uh, I got it.

259.t: Willie Hightower, who played ragtime and went to Chicago
259.s: Vincent recalls Willie Hightower playing with different groups before leaving for Chicago, and playing ragtime, though few could read it then.
259.q: So did he play ragtime? Yeah, yeah, he used to play ragtime. I was trying to remember if he could read it, you know. Very few of them was reading then. Yeah, he wasn't about to have him.

259.t: Big Kato and Little Kato, pianists
259.s: Vincent describes the two Katos as piano players, one a chord player who could barely read, the other a reader, and discusses their disabilities.
259.q: He said, what about Big Kato and Little Kato? Oh, well, Little Kato. You know him, huh? You know what I'm talking about? He was a piano player. Both of them piano. But Little Kato, he was a musician. He could have been there. And that's when I told him to play all those ninth cards and six cards,…

566.s: Humes recalls Nat Cole as a nice person who deserved his success, although Dance regrets that he played less piano as he became successful.
566.q: Didn't he though. And he was such a nice person.

566.t: Women pianists: Mary Lou Williams, Connie Berry, Nellie Lutcher, Rose Murphy
566.s: Humes names Mary Lou Williams as the greatest and lists Connie Berry, Nellie Lutcher and Rose Murphy as favourite pianists. Rose Murphy and Major Holley went to Ronnie Scott's after Humes.
566.q: On the piano I like Mary Lou and Connie Berry and Nellie Lutcher and Rose Murphy.

566.t: Irene Kitchings, Teddy Wilson's first wife and composer
566.s: Dance reports that Irene Kitchings died last year. Humes planned to record her songs such as 'It's the Little Things That Mean So Much'. Dance recalls Irene's own group in Chicago and then raises Roger Kellaway.
566.q: Yeah, well I was going to. "It's The Little Things That Mean So Much" that she and Teddy wrote.

566.t: Camille Howard from the 'Million Dollar Secret' record
566.s: Camille Howard, who worked with Roy Milton and played on Humes's 'Million Dollar Secret' record, has reportedly retired for religious reasons. Humes was looking for her and thinks a woman pianist would be fun.
566.q: Yeah, that's what I heard because I was looking for her.

566.s: Humes made a session with Ram Ramirez, who writes beautiful songs, can play when he wants, and is temperamental but nice.
566.q: Oh he wrote some beautiful songs. Now he can play when he wants to.

566.t: Pianists: Dave McKenna and Red Balaban's group
566.s: Beginning a run through pianists, Dance names Dave McKenna, whom Humes worked with once at a college concert in the East. She also worked with Red Balaban's group.
566.q: I'll tell you what else, Red Balaban took a group up somewhere there and I worked with him.

29.t: Princess Belle, the solo pianist at the Apex
29.s: Howard remembers Princess Belle, an older woman pianist who played alone at the Apex and taught him a lot when he played with her.
29.ch: The union and the 1920s-30s band scene
29.q: When I first got here? Oh, all I know was, they had somebody to be a -- something like a -- it was nothing, just like nothing. They had an entertainer, something. Now, that's Princess Belle. We forgot all about her.

29.s: Howard says Florence Cadrez was a fine pianist who worked jobs but not with him.
29.ch: Alma Hightower and other women musicians
29.q: Oh, she was a pianist, yeah.

29.t: Hightower on piano and in his first Los Angeles band
29.s: Howard says she played piano a little and sat in his first band, which played dances around 1906.
29.ch: Alma Hightower and other women musicians
29.q: That was when I was first gettin' started playin'. And all I could play was with the musicians, you know.

29.t: Princess Belle and other women instrumentalists
29.s: Willard asks about other women in Los Angeles music; Howard names Princess Belle, who played at the Apex.
29.ch: Alma Hightower and other women musicians
29.q: Huh? Yeah. I got it. Okay. Princess Bell was workin' down there. I was workin' down there, too-- (chuckle)--I was gettin' a job, hustlin' up a job, you know. I went around a hustle.

29.s: Howard praises Charlie Lawrence as a studious pianist who played everything, including Rhapsody in Blue and After Hours, and whom Lloyd Reese admired.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: Charlie used to play that. And then he played another one, a good one, too.

29.s: Collette and Howard praise Lady Wilcar, who played with Al Adams and George Brown's bands.
29.ch: Alma Hightower and other women musicians
29.q: What do I know about her (chuckle)? Lady Wilcar? She could play a piano, man.

1.t: Effie McDowell, Clarence Todd and the Jamaica old-timers
1.s: Milt mentions a singer from the Hall Johnson Choir who knew Clarence Williams, and Danny mentions Clarence Todd and an open-house family friend.
1.ch: Lu Barker and the Barbarin family
1.q: There's a man named Todd, Clarence Todd, who was a singer and a composer -- he lives out there. Did you ever check that name, of Clarence Todd? He was from here. His sister was named Camilla Todd; she was a songstress. Right here they've got Joe Gordon, who is from New York. He lived out there. He…

1.t: Barrelhouse pianists, the 'horses' beat and seeing King Oliver in a parade
1.s: He names early blues pianists, explains the 'horses' as boogie-woogie, and recalls following his uncles to see King Oliver's band at a funeral parade.
1.ch: Boyhood scene: halls and dance music
1.q: Black Nolan, Buckeye Wilford. What did they play? They played piano. All these were piano players? They played the blues, yeah, piano players. Black Nolan, Buckeye Wilford. Yeah, they were always welcome. Shine, regular hunky-tunk piano players. First time I heard what it's called now Boogie…

1.t: Willie the Lion at Pa and Jerry's
1.s: At Pa and Jerry's the Lion played intricate piano and Danny says arrangers borrowed his turnarounds, while Jelly Roll dismissed him as classical.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: And they had this upstairs, too, but it was a little crowded place, and it would get real smoky quick. And there was Willie Smith, the Lion, playing piano, playing his versions that was ahead of time. Like his things, "Morning Air" and all them pretty things he'd play at intermission, was…

1.t: Playing with James P. Johnson and Willie the Lion Smith
1.s: James P. Johnson and Willie 'the Lion' Smith, who praised Barker for knowing when to lay out behind a pianist, are the subject here.
1.q: Me and him were tight. I’d worked with James P. Johnson. I was tight with him. James P. Johnson . . . At that time I was working with James P. Johnson before I joined Benny Carter. Between Cab. James P. Johnson heard the record, Don’t You Feel My Legs, say, “You got a hit. I’m working with you.” He…

1.t: Joe Spaulding, the brilliant pianist with clipped wings
1.s: Danny and Milt recall pianist Joe Spaulding, who came with Eddie South from Europe and later hung around the Rhythm Club.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Yeah, Spaulding would come around the Rhythm Club, smile all night and (?), because he's talking about how great Spaulding was. And the man is this...you know, this...wings clipped, you know...

369.t: Basil Spears and Hazel Scott as entertainer
369.s: She recommends Basil Spears from New York, and says Hazel Scott looked beautiful at the piano and could move a room.
369.ch: School, women pianists and the Chicago style
369.q: Out of New York. And Hazel Scott was a good entertainer. She looked beautiful at the piano.

369.t: Lesser-known women pianists and singers, and the trio format
369.s: She names Camille Howard, Annie Laurie, Hadda Brooks and Nellie Lutcher, and says a trio lets you rest.
369.ch: School, women pianists and the Chicago style
369.q: Was Camille Howard a piano player or a singer? Well, Camille Howard was with Roy Milton. Annie Laurie. Hadda Brooks.

369.t: Pianists rated: Cleo Brown, Ellington, Basie, Garner, Waller, Lutcher
369.s: Brief assessments: Brown's left hand, Basie with Peterson, Garner the funkiest, Waller laid it down, Lutcher knew her strengths.
369.q: Ellington could play with his band. I guess he could stride a little bit, couldn’t he? Him and Basie.

369.t: Pianists rated: Jelly Roll Morton, Hines, Tatum, Raymond Walters, Teddy Wilson
369.s: She calls Tatum the master, Raymond Walters her drunken idol who showed her Tatum runs, and Teddy Wilson the Mozart of the piano.
369.q: Oh, he was my idol. He showed me how to play like Art Tatum. He stayed drunk most of the time but he sure could play.

369.t: Pianists rated: the boogie-woogie trio and Nat Cole
369.s: Meade Lux Lewis, Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons were all great heavy boogie players; Nat Cole played like Earl Hines.
369.q: He could play like Earl Hines. And who else did he play like? Yeah, he played like Earl Hines.

377.t: Bobby Henderson as one of his favorite pianists
377.s: Basie clarifies that Bobby Henderson, whom he first heard with Billie Holiday, was one of his favorites, along with James P. Johnson, the Lion and Fats.
377.ch: 1977: Kansas City honor and the piano
377.q: : Bobby was great. I didn't say he was my favorite, he was one of my favorites. I could never point out no one particular of my favorite for everything, because he was one of my favorite piano players.

377.s: Basie says he tried some boogie-woogie, heard in Kansas City, and names Pete Johnson, Albert Ammons and Meade Lux Lewis.
377.ch: The band, its players and singers
377.q: : I tried to do a couple of things with it, which is something that I heard a lot of in Kansas City and then I heard a couple of the top guys playing it, who really could play it.

377.t: Great accompanists: Bobby Henderson and Tommy Flanagan
377.s: Basie says no one played for vocalists better than Henderson and praises Ella's pianist Tommy Flanagan.
377.ch: 1977: Kansas City honor and the piano
377.q: Yes, and I don't think anybody could play for any vocalists any greater than he could.

377.t: A two-piano record with Tommy Flanagan
377.s: Basie calls Flanagan the most underrated pianist but says Tommy scares you; he had never thought about recording with him.
377.q: To tell you the truth, I have kind of [pianist] different feelings altogether. We haven't really did anything together. I mean we did a couple things -- Pete and I did a couple things, but we just (inaudible), you know. But Tommy and I haven't been that close. And I love him, you know. Right in the…

377.s: Basie says Hank Jones plays so much piano he would do everything for you, and he is still waiting for Hank to invite him to his house to hear him.
377.q: Hank Jones? It's hard to explain. Hank plays so much piano (unintelligible) Ain't no telling how much piano he plays. He's on top of everything. I mean, he's just (unintelligible) And (unintelligible) there's Hank sitting there, man. Both of them play as much piano as anybody. More.

31.t: Boston piano players: George Rickson, Dan Carey, Burroughs and others
31.s: After mentioning visits to a home for the blind, Whaley names reading and ear pianists from Boston.
31.q: George Rickson was -- he played for all the shows. See, when a man wanted a piano player for the show, they'd get George Rickson.

31.t: Joe Steele, the conservatory pianist, and Gershwin at the Lafayette
31.s: He describes Boston pianist Joe Steele, nine years at the Conservatory, who played Rhapsody in Blue at the Lafayette, where Gershwin kissed him.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: That's right. Joe Steele was a conservatory man. He and I went to the conservatory together, and I quit -- but he stayed there. He was in the conservatory nine years.

31.t: Pianists Edgar Hayes, Chitteson and Hank Jones
31.s: Whaley remembers Edgar Hayes's 'Stardust', the smooth accompanist Chitteson, and Hinton tells him Hank Jones is musical director of 'Ain't Misbehavin'.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: Oh, Edgar! Edgar was a very good pianist. He had a band, you know, and he went up to the -- he was up at the Cotton Club I think for awhile, with somebody.

31.t: Willie the Lion Smith and Duke
31.s: They agree the Lion had a great ego and Duke called him his mentor.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: Oh, Willie the Lion? Well, see, Willie the Lion was always like -- well, I never did come much in contact with Willie, but I knew he could play.

31.t: Joe Steele on the train, and Joe Jordan's gambling winnings
31.s: Hinton asks for more pianists, and Whaley adds Joe Steele and Joe Jordan, who won a fortune at Monte Carlo and built the Jordan Building in Chicago.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: At the Conservatory of Music in Boston, he was up there in the conservatory nine years, and I -- see, we used to ride on the train, because he used to work outside, he used to work in one of the clubs, see.

78.t: Earl Hines as Horace's piano idol
78.s: Asked about his piano style, Horace names Earl Hines his idol, recalling Hines' broken bass pattern, 'Sweet Lorraine', and following him in Pittsburgh.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: In those days, my idol was Earl Hines. And I used to watch Fatha whenever I had the chance, you know, because I would see him quite a bit, and he and my brother were very good friends, and they would sit down and talk music, and Earl would play. He loved to play a jam session and things, you know.…

78.s: Asked about Feather's claim that he was the more swinging Hines-style pianist, Horace says Fletcher played fast showpieces like Honeysuckle Rose while he preferred Sweet Lorraine-type tunes; he idolizes Fletcher's success.
78.ch: Setting the record straight on Hendersonia
78.q: Fletcher was a great pianist, and he always liked more or less to play things that had a fast beat, just the opposite of what Ben Webster was like. And it showed off his execution, and, of course, when people came out to see Fletcher, naturally Henderson, in this way he could be flashy in playing…

78.t: Arthur Lee Simpkins, and imitating Earl Hines with minor riffs
78.s: Simpkins sang on the floor and on the air and learned tunes quickly. Horace patterned his piano on Hines and used minor-key riffs in swing blues choruses.
78.ch: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
78.q: Yes. And he sang right on the floor, and of course, he was on with the broadcasting deal too, the sessions, you know, and he sang all the tunes, and he was great at learning the tune quick. This is what you had to do naturally, when you're (unaudible) broadcasting, and the guys were bringing in new…

78.t: Stuff Smith could talk while playing; Horace and Fletcher couldn't
78.s: Stuff Smith came from Alphonso Trent's band and chatted with the audience while playing; Horace, Fletcher, Erroll Garner and Earl Hines cannot talk and play.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: Oh, yes. Well, you know, Stuff Smith came from a great band Ant named Alphonso Trent. This is quite a few years back, but he had a swinging band. Stuff

78.t: Piano style: chords in ensemble, single line or octaves in solos
78.s: Horace played chords with the ensemble and single-note or octave lines in solos; Hines-style octaves worked on slow tunes like Sweet Lorraine but not fast ones.
78.ch: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
78.q: I would play chords when the ensemble thing was going, but as soon as you got to the solo, it would be the -- sometimes the one finger, and of course, Earl would play like in octaves, you know.

171.t: Countess Johnson and other women pianists
171.s: Countess Johnson replaced Mary Lou Williams with Kirk, died young; another woman pianist played across the street.
171.ch: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
171.q: There was another woman named Etta, or sump'n like that, played across the street from us who was the queen of all of 'em. She only played and sang alone. But she'd come into those jam sessions, and tear up some of those men. She and her husband just played it alone over in that little club and…

171.s: Her style fell between Earl Hines and Basie, fast and effortless; she never sang.
171.ch: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
171.q: No. See, we had Bill Nolan; he played drums and sang with us. She never sang.

171.s: Everett Johnson battled Pete Johnson all night and was for a time more popular.
171.ch: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
171.q: Everett Johnson was one of those cats that could get out there and stretch out on Pete Johnson, and they'd battle all night. Yeah. He could really play barrelhouse and play some eight-to-the-bar blues and all that, you know.

171.t: Earl Hines's influence everywhere, stretched tenths
171.s: Hines was the biggest piano influence after the barrelhouse players; rumour said his webs were cut to stretch tenths. Includes a hotel interruption.
171.ch: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
171.q: Uh-huh. Yeah, everything's all right up there. And so everybody all over the country was patterning after Earl Hines.

171.t: McShann's later study and piano style
171.s: Dance asks if McShann's conservatory study and Tatum changed his playing; Ramey notes the difference between solo and band pianists.
171.ch: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
171.q: Yeah, I can see he had quite a bit of improvement. I can see him more or less doing a lots of Tatum stuff, because I guess that's because he plays alone. As I said, there's two kinds of piano players, one that is -- where you're playing single, and where you're playing with rhythm sections it's a…

248.s: Dawson names Alfred Wilson, Tony Jackson and Robert Caldwell, none of whom he worked with.
248.q: They had another father there, but it was a good pianist. Well, maybe I can remember. I can't think of his name. Talking about Alfred Wilson. Alfred Wilson. Tony Jackson. Tony Jackson was a good pianist. Did you ever work? No. Did you ever work? No. Yeah, yeah. I never worked with them fellas.…

248.t: Camilla Todd, pianist with Hippolyte Charles, and where to find her
248.s: Dawson says Camilla Todd was a great pianist with Charles; the pair try to work out where she and her brother Clarence live, and suggest asking Sweet Emma.
248.ch: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
248.q: oh yeah Clarence Todd is still alive it's been about yeah it's been about three or four months ago I saw for real? or Canal Street yeah

248.s: Names of district pianists such as Jackson, Cahill and Winenboy are given, and Dude Robertson, now a guitarist, comes up.
248.q: well the rhythm sounds was pretty good you see and like what you call what's his name now Wilson, Cahill, Jackson Jackson was pretty good

248.t: Blues piano players who played alone
248.s: Dawson recalls a blind blues pianist and how solo pianists played limited keys and could not work with bands.
248.q: I met a fella up there for, uh, this old piano player, which used to play at them time. I can't think of his name now. But Clayton, know him good. He's blind. I happened to meet him. I played up there one night with Clayton, you know. And I saw him up there. What kind of piano player was he? Oh,…

622.t: Chicago pianists: Joe Sullivan, Stacy and Grunewald
622.s: They discuss why Chicago white pianists were weak, Joe Sullivan's emergence, Jess Stacy, and Grunewald's arranging at WGN.
622.q: And I can't remember when I first ran into jazz. He was sort of a legend to me for quite a long time. Art Grunewald, on the other hand, I don't want to not pay proper attention to him. He really was good. Probably still is.

622.s: Ashcraft calls Hines possibly the greatest pianist and describes his right hand, vibrato, tenths and Jimmy Johnson bass.
622.q: when I was saying for instance that Chicago pianists weren't much good I realized that I was being a little presumptuous really there were some wonderful pianists I mean Art Grunewald that we were talking about was of course really first class in many ways Roy Bargy there were some very very good…

622.t: Joe Sullivan's 1926 record and Chicago piano
622.s: Ashcraft says Sullivan's 1926 record was the first driving Chicago piano, though he does not link him to Chicago.
622.q: When I again talk about Chicago pianos, I drop out Joe, only because I really don't associate him with Chicago. That record in 26 was the first really driving piano that ever came out of Chicago.

622.t: Who the Austin group were, and their pianists Grunewald and Dave North
622.s: Ashcraft lists the Austin High players, and they discuss Art Grunewald and Dave North as pianists.
622.ch: Tenor sax and the Austin boys
622.q: I think Davey Tuff was there. Gene Cooper was at University High. Tash was at Austin. Jimmy and Rich were both at Austin. And Bud.

280.t: New Orleans piano players: Udell Wilson
280.s: Asked about unrecorded New Orleans barrelhouse pianists, he names Steve Lewis and Udell Wilson, a long-fingered Kansas City player who worked the downtown joints in the 1920s.
280.q: He played in all the joints, Texas Dancer, all them joints downtown. He was a great piano player. Yeah. Udell Wilson. Bad, long fingers. Yeah. Great piano player.

280.t: Little Willie and the unrecorded New Orleans pianists
280.s: Little Willie and Red held jam sessions; these men played everything with a strong left hand like a whole band, and none got to record. Terry Wilson took some of their style.
280.q: I believe so. Yellow. He had a brother called Yellow. Red and Yellow. They both played. Little Willie. Little Willie. Little Willie. Little Willie. What? Little Willie. That's all I know. Little Willie. He played here like Hell. Used to have jam sessions between him and the great guy. They was the…

280.t: Younger players and more names: Santiago, Joe Robichaux, Stackelia
280.s: They compare ages and go over more New Orleans names, including the Santiagos, Joe Robichaux, Charlie Hampton and Stackelia, whom Williams knew in the 1920s.
280.q: Yeah. It was two Santiago. Now I know the older one but this young one, I don't know. So you don't know Bono. I don't know. I don't know.

280.t: Barrelhouse names from the interviewer's list: Clayton, Dookie, Honey
280.s: The interviewer reads names of piano players; Williams knows only Clayton (piano and trumpet) and says others came after he left. He recalls Honey and Little Willie.
280.q: Played both, I know. Yeah. Clayton, he played piano and trumpet too. I think Clayton lived. No, he died recently. Did he? Yeah. He wasn't living. Sure, I know. Little Dookie. Dookie. Dookie. Dookie. What is that? Piano player? Yeah. That's how I made. Little Willie. I know Little Willie. Little…

293.t: Fish fries and early piano players: Deku, Chinese Charlie, Juby
293.s: Asked about back-alley fish fries, he names piano players Walter Deku, Chinese Charlie and Juby who played them.
293.ch: Piano players, Hot Springs and Chicago
293.q: Yeah, twenty years ago, the back alley fish fries. Back alley fish fries. Piano in the backyard. Did you play for yourself or? No, I just played the piano myself. You know, the honk-ton. What kind of numbers did you play? Well, we played mostly blues, you know, whatever I knew. I was playing good…

293.t: Piano technique, the district and Zeno's ballroom
293.s: Talk of black-key players, Ed Mercier, his visits to the district at age nine and playing piano at Zeno's ballroom.
293.ch: Pianists, the district and Stormy Weather
293.q: Yeah. You know. All of them... All of them hit them white keys. All piano players I know hit them white keys. You know. Play with the black keys. You know. You got to grow up on them, you know.

293.s: Praises his pianist Bunnell, who could imitate Earl Hines, Duke Ellington and others, and recalls practicing at Peterson's place on Claiborne Street.
293.ch: Orleans Pleasure Club to PWA band
293.q: Yes, indeed. He was the baddest piano player they had in the city in the Orleans. He was one of the best and couldn't really know. Fingers like Liv Rache. He could play just like Liv Rache in my book. You know what I mean? I'd say, just Albert and him play, I said, yeah I'm going to take me a…

293.t: Tony Jackson and other district pianists
293.s: Remembers Tony Jackson as a good pianist and singer, seen when fetching nickels from his uncle, and other pianists like Calvin Jackson.
293.ch: Orleans Pleasure Club to PWA band
293.q: Yeah, Tony Jackson, yeah I know Tony Jackson well. Oh you know him well? Yeah, he used to be around there. What I've seen I used to have to go in the bar to get my uncle to give him some money. When I used to go in there and say, you know you don't belong in here. I said, oh well it's alright. I…

650.t: Piano players Buddy Gurns and Sam Henry in the Gravier Street houses
650.s: Gurns was a Gravier Street piano player who taught him sporting house rags; Sam Henry played various houses, including Hattie Rogers's.
650.q: Oh, Buddy Gurns wasn't much. Buddy Gurns, he wasn't much. He was a pretty good piano player. Poor Buddy Gurns. Buddy Gurns, he wasn't much. He was a gravity street player. I don't think he'd ever been down playing no way. Down across Camar Street. Buddy Gurns.

650.t: Buddy Goins, Jockey Adams and other old pianists
650.s: Amacker recalls following Buddy Goins and Jockey Adams, now blind, and the interviewer asks about Robertson and Cato.
650.q: I get a bull. I get a bull. I make stick. Wow! Oh! . Gasket Street? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Buddy Goins, I followed Buddy Goins some years ago, putting a piano player. And Buddy Goins and there was Jockey Adams, a color fellow, and Jockey Adams prayed for the one night. Jockey's living now, but they say…

650.t: Good blues piano players and their repertoire
650.s: Amacker names the old blues pianists (Sam Henry, Kitchen, Ollie Sullivan, Birmingham) and the pieces and original blues like Jelly Roll Blues they played.
650.q: Sam Henry, a friend called Sam Henry, old timer. Another friend called Kitchen, he was his name. Sam Henry, Kitchen. And another one called Ollie Sullivan. And another one called Ollie Sullivan. In that day they were good blue players. In that day Kitchen, Sam Henry, Ollie Sullivan. And as you…

650.s: The pianists also played their own rags; Amacker describes a popular rag and who featured it, including Sam Henry and Lulu.
650.q: No. Most of them could play a lot of their own make-up rags. Hundreds of different kinds of rags. Used to be a rag in that day. A very popular rag in that day, I don't like to use the word, but a very popular rag in that day made a lot of money off it. Used to go to the shithouse rag. Same to say…

199.s: He recalls an uncle, Walter Lewis and Papa French.
199.q: Yeah. But he comes out of that same, that same period, yeah. Same period, same thing? Yeah, because I had another uncle, Uncle Tat, his brother, they called him Summer Ross, and he could play, man. They had several guys around there, man, those guys could play, man. And when you heard them you had…

199.s: He loved Oscar Peterson, Art Tatum, Nat Cole and Phineas Newborn.
199.q: Oh man, I like Oscar Peterson, man. I was crazy about Oscar Peterson. I saw the greatest piano player in the world, Teddy Wilson. Not Teddy Wilson. He was good. I met him down here in New Orleans. But his blind, Art Tatum.

199.t: Being featured on King Cotton and Pine Top boogie
199.s: He was introduced as Larry King Cotton in Washington, and remembers an uncle playing Pine Top.
199.q: The only time I had to play, the only time I had to play, when they featured me on that song I made, King Cotton. I didn't know I was even going to, they said, Cotton, you might be on the program. I said, okay, so we were somewhere. Washington, D.C. And this guy came up there and said, now ladies…

199.t: Professor Longhair and other New Orleans piano styles
199.s: He discusses Longhair's style, imitators, the Olympics and Dirty Dozen, and Tuts Washington.
199.q: I'm a real piano player. Yeah, he said, let me show you this, let me show you that. But my dad could play just as good as he could. Oh, really? Yeah. Stuff that he played, my dad could play that kind of stuff, yeah. Was he about his, your father about his oldest tuts? He would have been. He was, I…

137.s: They discuss Joe Turner, Pete Johnson, Julia Lee, other Kansas City singers and pianists, and Juanita Bolo.
137.q: There is something about that style of music that's distinctive. And I can't put it in words, though, I don't know what it was.

137.t: Moten as a pianist and the 1929 versus 1932 recordings
137.s: Moten read anything and played well only with music in front of him; the 1932 sides began to swing more.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: They started some swinging with that Morton Swing stuff. Might have been the rhythm section, they had a lot of changes they had to do.

137.s: Durham praises McShan's tempo sense and riffs as underrated, comparing him on piano to T-Bone Walker on guitar.
137.q: It's sleeping on him a little bit. He's original man, and he offers a good feeling and everything, and he's playing his thing. He's a T-bone walker on the piano just like T-bone on the guitar, Christian was -- yeah, because Christian picked up -- he moved on into the Eastern style along with…

137.s: Roosevelt recorded originals on a bad piano for Battle, singing and playing like Fats Waller, and the records never came out.
137.ch: Long Island years and Battle's estate
137.q: No, fool around with the records too long. He'd fool around. Got a lot of records on my brother and a lot of original songs. He sings and plays like Fats Waller, commercial tunes.

0.s: Caldwell doubts Earl Hines copied Teddy Weatherford; Glover Compton was more an entertainer at the piano.
0.ch: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
0.q: That's what type he was. Glover (unintelligible) -- used to go and see Glover. You know, he remind you Glover, a lot of Jelly Roll --

0.t: Willie Gant, an overlooked stride pianist
0.s: Willie Gant never recorded much, played cocktail piano at Rudy's, and was a stride player in the class of Fats and Willie the Lion.
0.ch: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
0.q: Well, he got that job down at Rudy's down there on Madison Avenue. He was down there for years after he, you know, he --

0.t: Casino Simpson and the Chicago pianists before Earl Hines
0.s: Chicago was big after Caldwell left; Casino Simpson, a Wilberforce classmate, imitated Fats Waller and Earl Hines.
0.ch: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
0.q: He was a fine pianist (unintelligible) -- we all came up together in school, Casino, Self, Homer, Cecil Irwin (unintelligible) --

0.t: Cliff Jackson's band at the Nest and the long-haired professor pianist
0.s: Personnel at the Nest and the pianist they called the Professor, who read everything and later went to Europe.
0.ch: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
0.q: See, in that band we had Preacher Jones on trumpet. We had Bethel H. Burke and Manzie Johnson, when we broke in, Samson Edgar Simpson.

90.t: Shepherd's Cafe and pianist Coot Davis
90.s: Sitting in at Shepherd's Cafe with his grandfather on bass, soulful drummer Skinny Thomas and blues pianist Coot Davis.
90.ch: Touring shows and the bands he heard
90.q: And there were so many different characters around through that period that I heard play, some fantastic players... Down on Neal Street in Jackson was a cafe called Shepherd's Cafe, and I used to go in there and sit in sometimes with Britt Roseby(?), and my grandfather played in there. The piano…

90.t: Wat Sanders' Blue Room in Tampa and pianist Chick Stephens
90.s: The band takes a Tampa job where he meets Art Tatum-class pianist Chick Stephens.
90.ch: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
90.q: And Bolden was drafted. So they decided to make me the leader. I was voted the leader of the band! So we stayed there, and played until we were approached about another job in Tampa, Florida, at a place called Wat Sanders' Blue Room -- the Blue Room, and Wat Sanders was the guy who owned it. And so…

90.s: Glenn's Barbecue's back-room sessions where he first met pianist Carl Perkins.
90.ch: San Francisco and the postwar slump
90.q: : Yeah! The fantastic pianist, Carl Perkins, one of the real geniuses of the instrument. And in fact, he had his own way of playing his left hand. He sat sideways

90.t: The Blue Flame and boogie-woogie player Bear Tracks
90.s: Joe Ketchum's Blue Flame club, and the barefoot boogie-woogie pianist Bear Tracks he later wrote a song about.
90.ch: Touring shows and the bands he heard
90.q: And then they had the Blue Flame, which was run by a very popular guy around home named Joe Ketchum(?). Now, that was... He named it after Woody Herman's theme song, "Blue Flame," when Woody first came out... Was it Herman or Shaw? Which one was "Blue Flame"? I think it was Artie Shaw, and "The…

174.t: Burnell Santiago as a small boy pianist
174.s: Dejan remembers Burnell standing on Coca-Cola boxes to play piano, alongside Lil' Willie, Baby Bruce and Walter Pichon, and compares him to a child star.
174.q: Yeah, when Burnell was small I remember taking a clap and then sometime I used to pass at a place on North Claremont and Santa Ann and used to put Burnell stand on two Coca-Cola box by the piano to play. At that time they used to call it Bucking one of them, you know, Lil' Willie used to go there,…

174.t: Burnell as soloist, speech impediment and improvising
174.s: He was better solo than in a band, had a speech impediment, and played unnamed tunes of his own that changed each time.
174.q: He was pretty good in a band but I mean he was better solo pianist by himself. He was not a good band man like Lester. See Lester was always a better band man than him, you know. He was a good band man. But just like you said, playing by himself, they couldn't touch him. They couldn't touch him,…

174.t: Montgomery's blues piano and Vivian from Kansas
174.s: Little brother Montgomery left in Omaha to record in Chicago; a Kansas woman pianist named Vivian replaced him and came back to New Orleans with the band.
174.q: Gee. We missed Brada for the blues that she could play, but we never missed them when she was playing in the band. She could play. She came all the way down here with us and played with the band a while and after things started to slow it up she went on back. But she was very good. In Kansas, huh?…

176.t: Early Florida piano players and ragtime
176.s: Billie names women pianists Willie Woods and Florida Beck, party-playing before bands, Josie in New Orleans, and Florida trumpeter Joe Jesse.
176.ch: Florida bands and New Orleans comparison
176.q: Yeah, plenty ragtime music. There was a girl named Willie Woods. Willie Woods. She was a great piano player. There was Florida Beck. She was a number one piano player. Was a woman? Yeah. Two women of course.

176.t: Piano players in New Orleans when Billie arrived
176.s: They discuss Williamena Bartlett, Jeanette, Edna Francis and Walter Decou, who played ragtime, blues and Spanish pieces.
176.q: Oh, I knew Williamena Bartlett. Oh, I knew Williamena Bartlett. Oh, I knew Williamena Bartlett. I knew Williamena Bartlett. Thank you.

176.t: Piron, the violinist and Steve Lewis at the Pelican
176.s: Neighbours Piron and the Mexican-looking violinist come up, then Billie recalls playing with Steve Lewis at the Pelican.
176.q: Steve Lewis and I used to call him up his uh, up over, let's see, at the Pelican, at the Pelican, Pelican up on Rand Paul Street. He had a, you know, saloon up there and thing like that. We used to go up there and play piano. We used to have some fun, me, Steve Lewis.

761.t: The pianist May who taught and was replaced by him
761.s: May played with Ridgley's band, read music strictly, and he substituted for her.
761.q: Well, she played with some bands too. I don't know May's last name, but she's a better tall girl, you may know her. She worked with Ridley Tuxedo, that's where I knew her from. I used to replace her when she was working with Ridley. When she lay off like that, I replaced her. That's how I got to…

761.t: Best pianists: Tatum, Wilson, Lewis, Pichon and Long Head Willie
761.s: Santiago names the best pianists, including his brother, Lewis, Pichon, Marvin and the ear player Long Head Willie.
761.q: Mm-hmm. Well, I think my brother was. I'd throw in bouquets out there. Yeah, I understand. A lot of people would say that.

761.s: He played classics, blues and jazz in a fast style close to Tatum and Waller.
761.ch: Brother Burnell and learning to read
761.q: No, he played all sorts of music, classic and everything. All numbers like a sophisticated lady. All hard numbers like body and soul. And he was wonderful. He could play blues and jazz too. He's a wonderful piano player. He could imitate anyone.

647.t: Steve Lewis self-taught; Robichaux and Pichon compared
647.s: Steve Lewis taught himself; John Robichaux; Joe stayed static; Walter Pichon was a genius.
647.q: He taught himself. He really taught himself. He had old man, at first it was old man, Robichaux helped him some, then old man Humphreys, Pierron helped him out a lot. And like Joe Robichaux, Joe Robichaux was a good piano player, but he wasn't too good a musician. He was like, I wasn't what you…

647.t: Playing a house-party number at the piano
647.s: Richards plays a number as he did and as he does now, and an ending Joe taught him.
647.q: Thank you. Very good. That sounds wonderful. That's part of his style. Let me see. Joe taught me one thing. Mm-hmm . That's the old part of the ending Joe taught me, but I forgot where they used to speak that ending.

647.t: Steve Lewis, Joe Robichaux and Walter Pichon as pianists
647.s: Only Steve and Joe influenced him; Steve sang vulgar party songs.
647.q: Because they were the only two of Walter. I never did pay too much attention to his style, of course he was coming along at that

762.t: Steve Lewis and the piano contest won by his friend
762.s: Asked about Steve Lewis, he recalls the boat contest won by his non-reading friend, and hearing Udell in honky-tonks.
762.q: Well I was pretty young and I didn't know too much about Steve outside he was a good piano player. And he could sing all kind of risky numbers and different things like that. And he played with P-Rone's band. But I didn't know too much about Steve. I saw him a couple of times. Because they had a…

762.t: Choosing his favorite pianist: his friend's genius
762.s: He names his non-reading friend the best, able to copy any record and improve on it, with Pichon's ideas also admired.
762.q: I wouldn't have to say Vernell was my favorite piano player, although he couldn't read. But there was nothing that he heard that he couldn't play. I mean when Earl Hines was popular, he would, when he'd sit down at the piano he liked the kid, he would listen on it and he was a lot of fun. And he…

762.t: Listening at ballrooms; Papa Crutch and Plutsem
762.s: He listened at ballroom doors, heard a boogie woogie player, was chased off pianos by Papa Crutch, and learned from the hunchback Plutsem.
762.q: Yeah. That's what they told me, that he used to make piano rolls. And we used to sit on the crib and the sidewalk and look in the ballroom, you know, they had these little doors that cut from the top and bottom. And I used to listen to these piano players. Then they had a place on the wagon top…

134.t: Sam Rivers and his wife Bea
134.s: Both praise Sam Rivers's far-out music, and Freeman recalls staying with him in New York and his years on the scene.
134.ch: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
134.q: When I go to New York, I stay with Chico. He’d always carry me to and from the gigs and to the airport.

134.t: Jack DeJohnette and Herbie Hancock from Chicago
134.s: Freeman says Jack played piano with him, and Herbie came from Evanston, not the clubs.
134.ch: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
134.q: Yeah, see, because they discovered him, and they made the hit Watermelon Man. He just – he started making movies, all kinds of different stuff. Of course he was with Miles Davis during Miles’s big years, when he had – what? – Shorter with him and Coleman, playing tenor.

134.s: They discuss Tatum's technique, Horowitz's admiration and Tatum's remark that he got it by practice.
134.ch: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
134.q: Yeah, because Horowitz was so great, he didn’t have to even play the music as written no more. That’s how great he was. He was like a great soloist. But you knew that he could play the music like it was written, if he wanted to. But he was a virtuoso.

231.t: What made Buck a good performer
231.s: Bubbles says Buck was great on piano, not as a performer, and insisted Buck come along on Porgy and Bess.
231.q: On the piano, man. No performer, because he couldn't do nothing in Porgy & Bess. I got him in Porgy & Bess with me because they couldn't get me without him, because I've got to work when the show ain't going to work and I can work with Buck without the show. Get my point? So I won't go on the show…

231.t: Buck's ragtime piano and his influence on Tatum and Peterson
231.s: Buck turned classics into ragtime, giving points to Art Tatum and Oscar Peterson; neither considered splitting after 40 years together.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: Making ragtime out of classics. Like "Souvenir from Woolworths," "Kiss me Again," Sextet from "Lucia di Lammermoer," "Hearts and Flowers," and "Clare de Lune," "Kiss me Again." Hit take all classics and make ragtime music out of them, you know.

231.t: Buck's genius and the birth of Buck and Bubbles
231.s: Buck played by ear, rivaled Tatum, Waller and Hines, and Bubbles conceived the act name Buck and Bubbles.
231.ch: Louisville, Buck and the carnival years
231.q: He'd hear it -- you'd whistle it to him, he heard it, you know what I mean. All that he didn't know already. Oh, he was a genius. He give Art Tatum a few bars. Fats Waller, he give these fellas a few bars of music. Earl Hines. He used to hang out with Louis Armstrong, you know. He got so he played…

70.t: Herman Chittison with Zack White and on radio
70.s: Chittison, with long fingers, played with Zack White, was on radio in Newport, Kentucky, and became a society pianist.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Herman Chittison was a wonderful pianist. He worked with Zack Whyte. He didn't stay with the band long after I was there because he had a radio program over in Newport News over there in Kentucky -- not Newport News but just Newport, Kentucky.

70.t: First pianists to impress him: Earl Hines and Fats Waller's pipe organ
70.s: He first heard Earl Hines with Louis Dippo's Pittsburgh orchestra, and had Fats Waller's 1926 Victor pipe organ record.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Well, one of the first pianists -- this will surprise a lot of people -- that I really heard that kind of made me listen -- I didn't hear him but once and then later on I heard him on a record -- was Earl Hines. He was playing with an orchestra out of Pittsburgh -- a singer named Louis Dippo. A lot…

70.t: Hank Jones, Oscar Peterson and Phineas Newborn
70.s: Jackson calls Hank Jones the complete pianist with a fine tone and rates Oscar Peterson and Phineas Newborn close to Tatum.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: That's right, full-fledged pianist. Any kind of piano you want, any kind of piano you want, Hank Jones can play it. I don't care -- If you want him to even go back to 1915, he can play that. Up till now, if you want him to play a vant-gark, he can play that.

75.t: Claude Hopkins and early Thirties swing pianists
75.s: Hopkins is called a light but effective stride pianist who deserved more exposure.
75.ch: Piano craft and the New York school
75.q: Light, but he was very effective, you know. He had that power (?) stride, and it was very rhythmic --

75.s: Profit played flatted fifths and ninth chords, between Fats and James P.
75.ch: Recent years and early piano influences
75.q: : It was like between J.P. Johnson and Fats Waller. Only he was more inventive, and he used to... His harmonies.... He was noted for his harmonies, the way he

75.t: Tatum could not accompany singers; Tatum at the Embers
75.s: Tatum overwhelmed Billie Holiday and the audience at the Embers; Horowitz said he wished he had Tatum's technique.
75.ch: Piano craft and the New York school
75.q: Well, he couldn't accompany a singer, I wouldn't say, because he couldn't subjugate himself to that. He himself used to sing like the way he plays, you know. He played for Billie Holiday, and poor Billie, you know; you just had so much piano being played, Billie couldn't... It's difficult for a…

112.t: James P. Johnson, Willie the Lion Smith and accompanying singers
112.s: He recalls James P. Johnson's burning piano at a matinee and compares Roberts, Johnson, Blake and the Lion as pianists.
112.ch: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
112.q: : But, I had the chance to meet all the great piano players down there. And that was a -- and then there was another one, James P. Johnson.

112.t: Lucky Roberts and Eubie Blake's advice about hands
112.s: Through Charley Johnson he meets Lucky Roberts, whose big hands and Junkman Rag amazed him, and Eubie Blake tells him not to throw his hands in the air.
112.ch: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
112.q: at that time had more instruments than the bands in the east. Because we was just beginning to take them on in the east. Because we had so much trouble with the -- oh, on account of the people in the summertime in Atlantic City, they stayed up and there was so many people. The cabarets were right…

112.t: Willie the Lion Smith in Newark
112.s: After leaving Brown he goes to Newark, where he fills in for Willie the Lion Smith who disappears for hours.
112.q: After I left Mr. Brown's place, I went to Newark. That's where I met another friend. A very good man that helped me so much. He's dead now. Willy Smith. But he was later known, (unintelligible). He gave him the title himself. Willy, 'the Lion', Smith. I used to go up there and play jobs for him.…

118.s: Russell asks about Udell Wilson, Emma Barrett, Mrs. Kimble and Mercedes Gorman; Williams doesn't recall them well, and says his mother played little outside church.
118.q: I think she rhymed with Selty. I don't know, I don't remember, for quite a while she played at a gig. Yeah, I think she played with Punch. Oh, with Punch? Once or twice I heard her with Punch.

118.t: Little Willie, piano contests and other pianists
118.s: Admired pianists like Little Willie, Mitchell Frazier and Steve Lloyd; Monday piano contests; others discussed.
118.q: Oh, he was a good piano man. Little Willie, sure man. Yeah, I used to admire him, he's playing, you know. Mm-hmm. During that time, uh, a friend of mine was playing, he did, and I called him Bunnell Sanago. Mm-hmm. And I'm catching to meet during that time and see who could outplay one another, you…

251.t: Pianists Peck Kelly and Alan Vann
251.s: Albert praises Peck Kelly and refuses to compare pianists such as Lloyd Glenn, Eddie Hewitt, Peck Kelly and Alan Vann.
251.ch: Later years and the Texas scene
251.q: Oh, Peg was great. He was a fantastic, I mean a great piano player. He was from Houston. But he used to come sit in a band in Chadland in the twenties. But Peg died recently.

251.t: A.J. Johnson, McNeil's Southern Syncopators and Lola Bell
251.s: Albert identifies pianist A.J. Johnson and the McNeil band, and blues singer Lola Bell who sang with his band.
251.q: I don't remember, there was a client that played, I haven't been able to call his name yet, that went to Europe. He was a member that day.

710.t: Fish fries and pianists Pelabon and Walter Pichon
710.s: Fish fries had no music but some houses had piano players, notably Eugene Pelabon, who played with his feet, and Walter Pichon.
710.q: Oh yeah, Fish Fry. Yeah well, Fish Fry don't have no music or nothing. Fish Fry. It's just entertainment amongst your friends. No music in Fish Fry. No music in Fish Fry. No music in Fish Fry.

710.t: Local piano players: Sweetie and Papa Deedah Da
710.s: Asked about solo pianists, Bailey names Sweetie, who no longer plays, and the interviewers ask about Papa Deedah Da.
710.q: Well yeah I didn't know right smart of them. This is Virginia Pellibon. Little fella called Sweetie. And this mom I couldn't call their name but I know a very smart of piano players.

10.t: Armand Hug and Don Ewell as Morton interpreters
10.s: Who might make a good album of Morton's music: Armand Hug and Don Ewell, compared on force and style.
10.q: Oh, I think he could. He played a wonderful piano the other night. I don't know if I heard that last one.

10.t: Scott Joplin's playing and piano rolls
10.s: Carew relays opinions of Joplin's playing and they discuss rolls labeled as Joplin.
10.q: Never recorded, no. Well, now I heard something different from that, to the truth, there's something that... late... No, no, no, no. A fellow from Indiana, Joe Russell Robinson. He commented on a tune that, St. Thomas Spencer's tunes that was played to some singer. He said, if you're listening to…

763.s: He praises a powerful pianist named Labosche who could break piano strings.
763.q: There's a piano player you should avoid. Oh, I'm done. He had a hand on that piano that when he was just mad and he played on that piano, he'd break the strings on it. No kidding. He was so sure of that piano. He would never play the piano like that. You should never see him playing like that.…

763.s: Talk of the late pianist Frank Cuehn who played in theaters and with symphony.
763.q: That is another... Another wonderful musician. Another wonderful pianist. Trying to think what band he was with when I came to town. Yeah. We were... We were... He played with symphony, he played in all these theaters, in the Palace Theater and all that. When I came, he was with Detroit on some…

268.s: After Lutton's he played piano for a group involving one of the Adams brothers near St. Charles.
268.ch: Big Eye Nelson, Lutton's and Adams
268.q: What did you do then? Yeah. Adams Brothers, I think one of them was playing up on St. Charlesbury. I don't know what they called it. Albert Clemler was playing drums and I was playing piano. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

268.t: Playing up and down for Bocage until the band ended
268.s: Bocage wanted a more active piano style. Turner stayed to the end of the band, his last.
268.ch: Day job, war and Bocage's band
268.q: Yeah, he said you'd live the piano player. You'd leave, you know.

620.t: Where the piano players came from; Sam Galata
620.s: Most pianists were born locally; he describes Sam Galata, who played only written music, near the alley.
620.q: Yeah, born and raised right here. there was a fellow downtown, I was forgetting him, they called Sam Galata. Sam Galata, yeah. Sam Galata was a good piano player, he played by notes. But he used to play all that kind of fashion music, you know. Didn't believe in playing no blues and all that. He…

620.t: The best piano players he heard
620.s: He ranks Frank Crump and Clarence Williams first, mentions George W. Thomas and his brother Juby, and Dwight Newman as later.
620.q: Well, I'm going to tell you. The best I heard play piano was Frank Crump for number one. I take Clarence William. Take Clarence William. And well, George W. Thomas, he could play, but he couldn't play, he wouldn't play much. He'd go more publishing and writing and publishing. Then they had another…

764.t: Peck Kelly the mystery man and boogie woogie pioneer
764.s: Manno describes Peck Kelly as an intelligent introvert, a boogie woogie pioneer, now going blind and devoted to classical music.
764.q: the New Orleans rhythm kings too no this was George Bichon and he played down there he was with Holly and there was another tenor man down tenor man down there name was Louie Thompson and he played oh he played the dirtiest tenor you've ever heard really real fine and he had he had some of the most…

764.t: Lazy Daddy, saxophonist Victor and the legend of Cook Shop Son
764.s: Manno knows none of the Black Texas pianists asked about, remembers only a saxophonist named Victor, and discusses the legendary Cook Shop Son.
764.q: no no uh in fact excuse me uh the only the only colored two colored musicians that I can remember in Galveston by name and one of them's name was Victor who was a saxophone player uh that was a a chauffeur for a wealthy family down there that left and he got into real big time I just what Victor's…

619.t: Helen Edwards, the pianist who transposed at sight
619.s: Pianist Helen Edwards, who died in California, could transpose any song for a singer; her sister read better than Billy.
619.ch: Lessons with Papa Tio and Helen Edwards
619.q: Go Re Mi Fa So La Ti Do. You had to sing it and play it. Play it, sing it. And he tell you play it just like you sing it. Well, this sort of girl had the band. She was at the Lyric Theater. One of the lyrical theater was in full bloom there with the old man Robichaud. Well, that was one playing…

619.s: He names Little Willie, Helen Edwards, Emma Barrett and others as the leading jazz pianists.
619.ch: Players and bands of old New Orleans
619.q: I'm gonna tell you. You had some good lady piano players. You had some very good men piano players. They had one little fella around here. He's called Little Willie. Played in my band for a long time. Never had a musical lesson in his life. Don't care what key you pick up, he could pick it up.

273.t: De La Houssaye: learning piano and the Audubon Street Four Plus One
273.s: Frank De La Houssaye, born 1933, taught himself piano and learned watching Archibald. He played in a college Dixieland band, the Audubon Street Four Plus One, before the Last Straws.
273.q: Well, they had an old piano at home that they used to lock up, but I used to get the key and open it and bang on it. And that's how I started when I was about 10 years old. And I've just been banging around on the piano ever since then.

273.t: De La Houssaye's favorite pianists and his style
273.s: He favors George Shearing, Fats Waller and Oscar Peterson, but his own style comes from Archibald. He plays chords on the beat because his left hand is limited.
273.q: On what instruments? Well, on piano first. George Shearing is my favorite. Quite odd here. This type of music. But I really do like George Shearing rather. And I used to like, well I still do like some of the works. Fats Waller, Oscar Peterson and some of those guys.

765.s: A young prodigy pianist, his style, early death, and attempts to reach his widow.
765.ch: New Orleans scene and jazz club
765.q: I don't think he was, but he used to sit in the arrogant and all. When you talk about piano players, there's a piano player that I'd like you to hear sometimes. He's a colored fellow. His name is Noel Fusher. He was raised with Lloyd Primm and all of us. Yeah, I don't know him. No, I don't think he…

765.s: Buck played chords by ear, steady beat, little soloing.
765.ch: Buck's Legion band and later gigs
765.q: Well, I mean, uh... He was hit and missed here, but I mean, uh... He had a good ear. Uh-huh. But I mean, he didn't know all the, you know, full changes. Uh-huh. And it helped, though. I mean, he, uh... He had that, uh, you know, steady, uh, full, full beat, you know? Yeah. And it helped a lot.

151.t: Playing two pianos with Nellie Lutcher
151.s: Allen asks about Reason and Nellie Lutcher playing two pianos at Sharon's at the Beach.
151.q: It was two pianos. See, what they had, a lot of places where, it wasn't a long, long time in Gay from Ingrace. But at Sharon's at the Beach there were two pianos. So Nelly was playing one side to another. During that time was the same time when Underneath the Harlem Moon came out. You remember that…

151.t: A church pianist and the Bulls Club
151.s: Reason tries to recall a piano player who played in churches and taught school.
151.q: Um... Um... I'm missing out with this piano player's name. He started playing for churches. I can't remember his name. And then that's when Alvin Alcorn had just started. Because he was in that band. This was a piano player? Uh... He was a piano player at his band. Uh-huh. And he used to hire other…

276.t: Steve Luce's record and playing on Charters Street
276.s: Nash recalls a pianist who recorded That Oughta Get It and played at the corner piano place on Toulouse and Charters.
276.q: I think Steve Luce made a recorded record of that, That Oughta Get It. That's where they go. Did it have words on there? Yeah it had words too. I just can't remember. Steve Luce recorded a record of that. Used to play out here on Charler Street.

276.t: Drive 'Em Down, the roving piano player
276.s: Nash knew the pianist Drive 'Em Down, who played in any honky-tonk with a piano and hung out at Liberty and Perdido.
276.q: Drive him down anywhere that had a hunker-tonk, that's where he played. Anywhere where piano was. Sure had no drive him down.

628.t: Piano players around when he was coming up
628.s: Williams names the pianists of his youth, including Noonie Perez and the Frazier family, and says Lil Dave Williams started with him.
628.ch: Beginnings and early New Orleans scene
628.q: The piano players? This boy here, Noonie. Noonie Perez, who was a, Bauhaus piano player. Because I was playing with Son Wilson then, trumpet player and that was, he's a piano player. And they real tunk, you know what I mean? Yeah, I know. Real tunk, yeah, yeah. I know from, and Simon, Simon, Boynel…

628.t: Dance halls and piano players like Plutzum and the Fraziers
628.s: Talk of Economy Hall and dance promoters, then more pianists: the humpbacked Plutzum, Simon, Mitchell and Boynell Frazier, and Red Toots.
628.ch: Beginnings and early New Orleans scene
628.q: He was humpback, red, and a little short neck like that. He used to play very hard. Plutzum.

23.t: Raymond Burke recordings and Jim Kweskin session; Armand Hug... Naki Parker on piano
23.s: Rose recalls an unsuccessful session with Jim Kweskin featuring Burke, then praises pianist Knocky Parker's knowledge, taste and ragtime playing.
23.ch: Opinions on players and ensemble jazz
23.q: That's right, exactly. And prefer to for that matter. Of course I've recorded Rayman a lot. I had that awful session with Jim Queskin, the jug band musician, a couple of years ago. I never had a chance to hear that for some reason. Well, you haven't missed anything, because this man just is not of…

23.t: Pianist Steve Pretorius and ragtime festival
23.s: Rose and Allen discuss young pianist Steve Pretorius, whom Rose heard at the Scott Joplin Festival in Sedalia.
23.q: You've probably never heard. Steve Pretorius. Well Steve Pretorius is a fine piano player. I did hear him in Sedalia in July at the Scott Joplin Festival. And he's a phenomenal piano player. I think he won fourth prize.

279.s: Hug names Jelly Roll, Earl Hines, Fats Waller, Jess Stacy and others as influences on his style.
279.q: I think that, well, of course, like I said, the New Orleans style was the musicians and the music of New Orleans was the greatest impact, accepting that as time, as I got older, well, of course, naturally I started advancing a little bit, you know. And listening to different musicians, we naturally…

279.t: Later influences: Hines, Stacy, Wilson, Waller, Tatum
279.s: Hines most revolutionized his style, followed by Stacy, Wilson, Waller and Tatum.
279.q: I think that the first real impact that hit me, when I say impact, I was already going under the influence of the old timers like Jelly Roll and the ragtime pianists. And I had one pianist around here by the name of Buzzy Williams, who was very, very excellent, and he gave me a lot of encouragement…

48.t: Best pianists: Weatherford, Hines, Zinky Cohn, Lil Armstrong; Albert Nicholas
48.s: He names Weatherford as best pianist, plus Hines, Cohn and Lil Armstrong.
48.q: The best pianist I remember was Weatherford, about the best pianist. I played with him at Rich Carlton, and he was about the best piano player I played with around. I played with Earl Hines a little. I played one or two jobs in Earl Hines. And this Zinke Korn. Oh yeah. I played with him. I heard…

48.t: Albert Wynn, Jasper Taylor and Dave Payton
48.s: Chicago trombonists and the pianist and arranger Dave Payton.
48.q: Yeah, he took a couple of lessons. He didn't stay, but he took enough to learn to play pretty good. He plays pretty good.

49.t: Piano players of the district: Steve Lewis and Piron
49.s: He names Steve Lewis and others as the best pianists back of town and says Lewis played with Piron.
49.q: Steve Lewis, uh, this Jackson, Udell, I don't know what his last name was, he played back there. Oh, there was, there was a, there was a, there was some white fellas played back there, I think Buzzy Williams played back there. Uh, but the, the, the, the three that I can remember the most was Steve…

49.s: They talk about pianists Bill Whitmore and Mickey Markle, the only pianist recorded with the Halfway House band, and Abbie's liking for rags.
49.q: I played with him. Mickey Markle is the only one outside of this one record of Red Longs where he made his own tune. Mickey Markle is the only one that ever recorded with a Halfway House band. That was Oscar's brother. He's got a place up here in Holman now I think he owns tourist camps and things…

286.t: Women pianists and two trumpets with two bands at the Pelican
286.s: Discussion of Miss Kimball, Mercedes Gormand and women pianists; at the Pelican two bands played, one in each corner, with two trumpets.
286.q: Mercedes Gormand. Yeah. When you—I thought we had most of the time was women's piano players. We had one or two men's piano players around there.

286.t: Nola band becomes the Silver Top band under old man Dutrey; pianists
286.s: Old man Dutrey took over and renamed it; he played clarinet and sax, the band added piano, usually a woman pianist.
286.q: Yeah. This boy just died there a couple of months ago, a couple of years ago. He was saxophone playing. That's when he started increasing the band, when the Pelican opened up.

634.t: Blind pianist Rosebud and Clarence Williams at Big Du Bois
634.s: A blind teacher, Rosebud, played piano at Big Du Bois's tonk, near Howard Avenue; Dick asks about his era.
634.q: Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. a blind teacher called Rosebud, and he used to play at Big Du Bois, Calvary. Well, he was playing piano and I was playing piano.

634.s: Brief talk about when boogie woogie began in New Orleans and the number Hopscotch Blues.
634.q: I couldn't play piano. Just play out my money. And put a whole lot of stuff in the end and they started calling it a Boogie Woogie. And they picked up from that.

127.t: Blues pianists and surviving figures from the district
127.s: Allen and Punch discuss blues piano players, a woman pianist on St. Peter, and whether Mrs. Tom Anderson is alive, before a break.
127.q: This woman right down on this street. What street we on? St. Peter? Yeah right down there. She used to be a piano player in the nightclub. Larry know her name good. You know who I'm talking about. She lived 10, 1010 I believe. St. Peter. Johnson I think. Yeah well she used to play in the nightclub.

127.t: Piano players in the Miramac band
127.s: Punch struggles to name the band's several pianists and recalls James Hemingway as a good one.
127.ch: Musicians he knew and played with
127.q: Well, we had two, three, had a girl. That girl I told him about went nuts, Laura. Laura. Made her a long time. Then we had a fellow named Brownie, Clowns Brownie. Oh, two, three piano players. They didn't keep no good piano. Oh yeah, the boy died. James, James from Atlanta, Georgia. Johnson, James…

484.t: Frank Froeba, the piano player Fletcher Henderson admired
484.s: Brownlee names Frank Froeba as one of the greatest pianists, able to play jazz and orchestra, with honky-tonk piano recordings.
484.q: one of the boys that I thought was one of the greatest was uh Frober lived out on Canal Street was it Jack Frober Frober or Frank Frober

484.t: The four-piece combo at the Ritz and pianist Frank Panera
484.s: A small combo at Jimmy Moran's Ritz with Pinky Gerbrek and Monk Hazel; they try to recall the pianist, eventually Frank Panera.
484.q: well I think that Frank Frober was one of the finest then uh I'm trying to think Pruitt not Pruitt what was his name played with us at the Ritz and uh Johnny Laporte was on drums and uh the old Monk Johnny left and Monk played uh played drums did Monk ever tell you about the the old man used to put…

766.s: He preferred Georgie Parker on piano, Paul Barnes on sax, and played with George Lewis and Big Eye Lewis.
766.q: A saxophone player, I mean, when I first started I'd rather work with Paul Bones than any of them. That's what I'm telling you, at his time, I mean. At his time, I mean, I'd rather work with him in a good piano. He'd play some ball in his time. Yeah, he was a good saxophone player, I mean. If that…

766.t: Neighbouring camp with Walter DeCue and Red Dugard
766.s: Next door to Moreau's, Walter DeCue and Red Dugard played, all old-time musicians.

58.s: Punch names the few pianists he knew, such as Steve Lewis and Walter Pichon, and Willie Smith.
58.q: Yeah. Nobody stuff with stuff Now Steve, he was with P-Rone, and Robichardt a piano player at the Lyric Theater. And Miss Todd used to play with the Tuxedos. Well now they had a big band, but all the rest of them bands used with five pieces and you had no piano.

58.t: Pianists: Manuel Manetta and Steve Lewis
58.s: Punch says bands used no piano, praising Steve Lewis.
58.q: Yeah. Like, we'd go up to the Audubon, Turon, places like that where they'd need piano players. He'd play with us up there. He was a real good piano player. But otherwise, we didn't use no piano.

707.t: New Orleans pianists and their styles
707.s: He names the old-time pianists he knew, Steve Lewis, Fate Marable, Udell Wilson, and the great Cooney Vaughn of Hattiesburg.
707.q: Well, practically I knew practically all the old timers around. Steve Lewis. Yeah. Walter Pigeon, Fats Pigeon, and Red Caillou, Udell Wilson.

707.t: More blues pianists in the South and Chicago
707.s: He names pianists such as No Leg Kenny, Albert Ammons, Cripple Clarence Lawson and songwriters still around Chicago.
707.q: Yeah, and they had a piano play along, yes, when I was a little boy riding all these, was a great... When they... his name was Ford, I didn't never know his other name. Ford. That was his name, and then they had another one played in Boca Lucey, they called Charlie Mahana, he was a great, great…

303.t: Red Mackey, Gene Austin, and Coco and Candy
303.s: Red Mackey's piano, Gene Austin as a 'black key man', and playing with Coco and Candy at the Spotlight.
303.ch: Pictures, Crescent City Jazzers and friends
303.q: You know, Gene Austin was a black key man. Mm-hmm. He couldn't play any white keys on the piano. Played all in F sharp and D flat and then E natural and all.

303.s: Photos of Sharkey and Alec Templeton at a packed Blue Room night, and Riddick's friend Joe Reichman.
303.ch: Scrapbook: Sharkey Bonano years at the Famous Door
303.q: I think. Officers Club at the NAS. It's Shipman. This... This... Algears Naval Base. Or... Some... You know, somewhere. I'd have to... I'd have to just go into all of the details to remember where they were. Yeah. This is at Blaise D'Antonis' home. This building was separate from his house. Does he…

767.t: Ida Cox, Skinny, and pianists who could not read music
767.s: Talk of Ida Cox and a self-taught pianist called Skinny leads to the interviewer's remarks on great New Orleans and Texas pianists of the 1920s-30s who could not read.
767.q: Incidentally I see where she gotta write up where she stuff Yeah, she cut out and cut some records again. I'd like to hear that. I played for her. And that little boy out of Houston, I don't know if you remember him, dog, my name was Skinny, he couldn't read but he could play the best piano player…

767.t: Lazy Daddy, Claude Kennedy, and pianists who played by ear
767.s: Discussion of the pianist called Lazy Daddy (Henry Fillmore) in Houston: his character, his skill with shows despite not reading, and Claude Kennedy leaving Troy Floyd's band.
767.q: Well just tell me a little bit how you played and you mentioned that, what did you say that his real name was? Henry Fillmore.

85.t: What set Teddy Wilson's playing apart
85.s: Carter says Wilson was the closest thing to Art Tatum, with taste, technique and harmonic sensitivity.
85.q: Well, I had also heard, although I hadn’t played with, Art Tatum, and I felt at that time that Teddy Wilson was the closest thing to Art Tatum at that time, you know. Gee, I don’t know. He had the taste and the technique and the fluidity and the harmonic sensitivity; many things about his playing…

85.t: Legendary stride pianists who never recorded: Sam Weber, Seminole, Putney Dandridge
85.s: Carter recalls obscure Harlem stride pianists and doubts that Duke Ellington took part in that circle.
85.q: I believe it was from Brooklyn, and his name was Sam Weber [phonetic]. And, if I’m correct, he was blind or partially blind. He was quite a pianist. He used to sit in with Willy “The Lion” Smith and Fats Waller and all of those guys, and he could always hold his own, you know, with them. I believe…

16.t: Stride piano and the pianists of his youth
16.s: He names James P. Johnson, Willie the Lion, Fats Waller, Clarence Profit and Herman Chittison and the wider flowering of jazz around him.
16.q: Well now there were all … when I came up, what a lucky time, what a lucky time. There were people that did all kinds of things. You know stride piano, James P. Johnson and Willie the Lion were great exponents of that. Fats Waller I think studied

16.t: Art Tatum, Erroll Garner and Fats Waller as influences
16.s: He heard Tatum, Hawkins and Webster at after-hours spots; Tatum pushed him toward writing; he compares Garner's percussive style with Waller's stride.
16.q: Stride piano and mostly Fats, I loved Fats Waller and I loved Art Tatum. As a matter of fact, at one point when I, before I finished the Juilliard School, I was going down to a place called George's Tavern, working with a guy by the name of Leonard Ware who used to be, who was one of the, he had…

505.t: Aydin Esen, the unknown genius pianist
505.s: Liebman praises Turkish pianist Esen and recalls a disorganized Columbia date with Dave Holland and Peter Erskine.
