505.q: He was unbelievable at synth. He was unbelievable on piano. We did – I did a record with him a couple years ago with Steve Smith and Anthony Jackson called Flashback [Flashpoint]. We did it out here at Red Rock, a couple minutes from here. Ayden is a genius.

505.s: Liebman recalls a live date with the young German pianist-composer Florian Ross, whom Kirchner thinks underrated.
505.q: This is when he was very young. He is a great musician. That was, I remember, live. We did that live. The first night was completely out. Second night was perfect. I came off the plane first night. I was out of tune. I was screwed up. We had a long conference the next day. I said, do a couple of…

528.s: Tyner discusses Hines's creativity and the era when a stride pianist was the whole band.
528.ch: Jazz Roots and the piano masters
528.q: In the time period that he came along I think he did a lot. He was animated, he was a very strong player in his genre, he was very creative. The stride piano was very important. I mean a matter of fact, a lot of piano players during that period . . . that was the band! You put a piano up here and…

528.s: Tyner calls Garner a one-man band and recalls solo piano gigs.
528.ch: Jazz Roots and the piano masters
528.q: Yeah Erroll was something (laughs) he really was a band unto himself, and the way he played, gee whiz. The octaves would be . . . he was all over the piano, he was something man, he was an entertainer. He came up in a period where the piano was the band, that was it and a lot of those guys came up…

80.t: Caroline Thornton, the pianist who led the Howard band
80.s: She could write out a part with one hand while playing with the other in the pit; she died in a car accident on the way to visit him in Philadelphia.
80.q: I've seen her play piano with one hand and write out a part with the other -- in the pit! And the show's going on. And when she hands it to you to play, it's right. Don't worry. It's right. That's how good she was. And oh, man, I was -- just the thought of working with her meant so much to me, and…

80.t: Sam Price as pianist and 'genius' organizer
80.s: Autrey calls Sam Price a hard-driving jam pianist and a salesman who could sell the Empire State Building, who often called him for record dates.
80.ch: Postwar years, accident and lean times
80.q: Well, he's a good jam artist. He kicks the hell out of what he knows, or what he does. He does it damn well. I've got to give the man that, you know. No, I -- uh, hmmm, well --

4.t: Edna Hightower, pianist in Kansas City and Los Angeles
4.s: Willard asks about Alma Hightower; Spikes recalls Edna Hightower as pianist in the Kansas City show around 1910 who later led the Hightowers Orchestra in Los Angeles.
4.ch: Later ventures, lodges and San Francisco recollections
4.q: Well, Edna Hightower--I told you--when we went to Kansas City to play in that theater, she was the piano player there. This is 19 and, uh, oh, '9 or '10. She was the piano player, and the other people were men. Then, after she came home...she came here in

4.t: Ragtime piano players Spikes heard in his travels
4.s: Spikes recalls ragtime pianists in the West, including Gene Thomas, Wesley Fields, Sid LaProtty and Jockey Bill of Prescott, and says it was all blues.
4.ch: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
4.q: No, they wasn't playin'...they called it ragtime in those days. All the piano players was ragtime piano players, y'know. They played all like Scott Joplin and those guys, y'know. They played all ragtime. Strictly ragtime.

9.t: Joe Steele, pianist who guarded his hands
9.s: Joe Steele, whose sister taught Holmes in Sunday School, played classical and dance piano, protected his fingers carefully, yet loved baseball.
9.q: : of his sisters was my Sunday School teacher when I was a little boy. And Joe was a great pianist, at that time playing Classical Music and dance music, as it was called in those days -- just the beginning of Jazz. The name "Jazz" wasn't used in all families. So he was a great dance pianist.

9.t: Joe Steele plays 'Rhapsody in Blue' for Gershwin
9.s: Holmes relates hearsay that Steele played the whole Rhapsody at an audition for the show 'Rhapsody in Black' and Gershwin said he needed no instruction.
9.q: : Well, they were putting on a show. "Rhapsody In Black" was the name of the show. An all-Negro show. And Gershwin provided the music. So they were using Gershwin's "Rhapsody In Blue" in the show. Now, this goes way back to the early Twenties, and "Rhapsody In Blue" at that time was not so popular…

379.t: Latin jazz pianists: Rodriguez, Lee Russell and others
379.s: He compares Rodriguez and Lee Russell and names other Latin players.
379.q: Yeah, and after that he'd go for the small group, and -- or lounge work, and maybe he'd go (unintelligible), but it never materialized to nothing. Another Panamanian piano player that came later was Rivera.

379.t: Cuban piano style and great pianists
379.s: He describes piano as bass and harmony and praises Benito.
379.q: Now, I'm glad you brought that up. When these people started fooling around here, and they're trying to deviate the people mentality and calling our music the piano players, they (unintelligible). And every piano player here, or every orchestra here, when you hear a piano play behind the band, or…

453.t: A local pianist who embellished popular songs
453.s: Randolph recalls a pianist (Benton Overstreet, he thinks) who improvised ornaments on popular songs.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: : No, there wasn't any. I had one fellow around there. He played, but he played piano and he was doing -- what was he doing? Da-da-da-da -- Benton Overstreet, I think. Did you know -- did you ever hear of Benton Overstreet? I think Overstreet wrote that.

453.t: Ragtime and Blind Boone: what he knew of St. Louis-area piano
453.s: DeMichael asks about ragtime repertoire and Blind Boone's piano rolls; Randolph knew Boone only from his mother's talk.
453.q: I didn't get a chance to hear him but I heard my mother talking about him. They say he was a wonderful pianist.

91.t: New York as the center for pianists
91.s: Fats Waller, J.P. Johnson and Willie the Lion show New York was the pianists' home.
91.ch: Harlem scene and race in music
91.q: Well, I don't know. The interesting thing about New York jazz, though, was look at the pianists that came from New York -- Fats Waller, J.P. Johnson, Willie 'the Lion' Smith, you know, from Newark, originally, but he really came up in New York, I think.

91.s: Carter calls Tatum a sacred cow who dazzled and moved him.
91.q: Like Untouchable? Yeah, I don't know -- it's very hard to criticize anything that he did. When he came on the scene, he was such a blockbuster. I mean, no one had heard anything like Tatum. And like I heard a musician, as I had mentioned probably in an earlier part of this interview, Monroe Burger…

92.t: Putney Dandridge's bass lines at the Radio Inn
92.s: At the Radio Inn on 18th Street, he heard Dandridge's beautiful piano bass lines, which influenced him.
92.ch: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
92.q: In other words kind of check up on the heritage, you know. I am very -- as you know, as I told you before -- chord conscious. But I have a -- you mentioned something to me that I had forgotten about working in Chicago with Elbert Topps.

92.t: Detroit pianists who sounded like Art Tatum
92.s: Collins names Willie Hawkins of Detroit and Lanny Scott of Cleveland as pianists who sounded like Tatum, and mentions Al McKibbon and Kelly Martin.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: It was Capitol, yeah, yeah. I also want to go back to Detroit, we were talking about Gerald Wilson (up there) when we picked him didn't we. And at this time I met a pianist who played so much like Art Tatum, his name was Willie Hawkins. And he finally came out here but he got ill and he went back…

19.t: Toby Walker playing I Got Rhythm for five dollars
19.s: Walker played a fast stride I Got Rhythm for an hour whenever the crowd paid, drinking with one hand and striding with the other.
19.ch: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
19.q: All of this was in this learning process of me meeting some of the greatest musicians in the world, and a lot of times not even being aware of just really how great they were! But all these people used to come...if they came to Washington, they came up to Freddy Woods' place.

19.t: Washington pianists Harold Francis and Dick Hopkins
19.s: Harold Francis was the most literate local pianist and showed him Wilson's style; Hopkins played like Earl Hines.
19.ch: Piano influences: Teddy Wilson, Tatum and Bud Powell
19.q: In the interim of this, there were some pianists around town that I liked very much. There was one guy, a fellow from New York who had come down here and he made Washington his home for a number of years. His name was Harold Francis. Later he worked with the Ink Spots for a while. I think he died…

8.t: Pianists he has enjoyed working with
8.s: Garland names Lil Hardin, Alton Purnell and others, and says many players claim to have played with Ed Garland.
8.q: I don't know if you heard of him, Henry -- ah, Henry's name? Wonderful piano player when I was on KFI.

8.t: Tricky pianists: Hines and Don Ewell
8.s: Hines changes keys without warning, and Garland describes how he and Don Ewell traded signals for breaks over twelve years.
8.ch: New Orleans style and bass playing
8.q: to be playing in A flat and he jump way down to D flat, you know, jump back into C. Oh, he's tricky, you got to watch him, know what you're doing.

237.t: Jimmy Jones, a young pianist at the Yellow Front
237.s: Goodwin remembers the young Jimmy Jones as a great pianist who played the Yellow Front.
237.ch: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
237.q: Well after he got here he didn't want to leave because he could gather up a whole lot of -- there was a lot of things going on. There was a little guy where -- we had mentioned a place called the Yellow Front. There was a little guy down there, young fellow, very young, Jimmy Jones, which God rest…

237.s: Smith and Lovett note ragtime piano is a dying art and remember Fess Hill playing it.
237.q: This old fellow that played the other night, what was his name, old piano player, ragtime piano player -- Blake.

76.t: Replacements at the piano: Big Boy and Gene Anderson
76.s: Zutty brought in a huge pianist called Big Boy, who later went to Canada; when Big Boy left for an act he got Gene Anderson, formerly of the Carroll Dickerson band.
76.ch: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
76.q: I brought in old Big Boy. Because Andy said, my God, he said, I didn't want you to, a piano player, but you brought me a piano mover. (LAUGHTER).

76.t: Marge's piano playing and Club 47 in California
76.s: Zutty says Marge played well in the band, and Doc Randall and Nappy Lamare, owners of Club 47 in Los Angeles, praised her walking-bass left hand when she sat in.
76.ch: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
76.q: Yes, she was playing piano in the band. Yes, she was playing good. A lot of guys in St. Louis would really brag on Marge, said, good piano player. And like Doc Randall, when I was playing at the Club 47 in California, Doc Randall, he was one of the owners of the place, he was a saxophone player.…

238.t: Cleo Brown's records and the demand for women pianist-singers
238.s: Cleo Brown's boogie records and Hollywood booking made women pianist-singers in demand, which she says helped her.
238.q: Yes, she was very well known. She really made her -- got her recognition on records. In fact she was responsible for the change, you know, and for the demand for women piano players and singers. Because before that time -- and she was doing a boogie woogie thing, you know, and before that time I…

238.t: Cleo Brown and the girl piano-singer trend
238.s: Cleo Brown's records began a trend for girl pianist-singers, and people expected Nellie to sing when she reached California.
238.q: Cleo Brown was very popular when I first came to California. You see, she -- before I left Louisiana, as a matter of fact, she was, you know, just -- she had made a record called, 'It's a Heavenly Thing,' and this -- she sort of started the trend really for girl piano players, you know, piano…

175.t: Burnell Santiago, the neighbor pianist, and Earl Hines
175.s: His next-door neighbor Burnell Santiago had a remarkable left hand, impressed Earl Hines, imitated others and died young.
175.q: No, there was no admission. But you could always find music going on right there. There was always a piano and any time you found a piano there was always a piano player. And that's how I used to remember this Burnell San Diego so terribly well. Oh yeah, that's right.

402.t: Reel 3: Gordon Kirst's band, the Blue Room and Armand Hug
402.s: Sal tells how Gordon Kirst was made bandleader, the first band in the Blue Room, and Armand Hug's rise as a pianist.
402.ch: WPA band and 1930s New Orleans bands
402.q: So naturally, Steve got to play. I don't know. So naturally, Steve got on me in the band to play piano. They all hung up to play piano in the band, not the Blue Room, see. I was the first band in the Blue Room, before I started going to name bands, you know, name bands. The same thing happened at…

35.t: Don Ewell's piano, Bunk's praise, and unrecorded tunes
35.s: Don Ewell's Jelly Roll style and four-beat left hand, Bunk calling him his number one pianist, and an unrecorded tune the band played.
35.q: Well, he's a piano player from Baltimore, uh, plays many, well, he has a way, uh, a style which, uh, uh, uses many of the stylisms, uh, uh, from the jazz tradition. And, and, uh, at that particular time, uh, he was very much on a jelly kick, and, and, uh, we used to stand behind the piano when he…

768.t: Hearing Jelly Roll Morton and her loud supporting piano style
768.s: Hearing Jelly Roll Morton made her play hard; the New Orleans men preferred her supportive playing and Oliver objected to her getting fancy.

769.t: Joe Robichaux and Alton Purnell on piano; Kid Howard before the English trip
769.s: He calls Robichaux a good modern pianist and Purnell a fine jazz pianist; Howard was brought back before England.
769.q: Well, he had stopped for a while and we went back and got him. Mm-hmm. So we had to go over… Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

243.t: Burnell Santiago as a boogie-woogie pianist
243.s: Breaux describes the pianist's gifts, his ear, his win against Earl Hines in a piano contest, and his boogie-woogie style.
243.ch: Paul Barbarin and his own bands
243.q: Could he play? His bass is alive. He's a boogie-woogie. Yeah, he played a lot of piano. I mean, he was... I'd say just naturally gifted because he couldn't read. But he could... He could improvise so well. And then... Then Barnell had such a keen ear. He could work in anybody's band. And I don't…

246.t: Piano players who sat in at suppers and parties
246.s: Glass names Walter Deco and Harold Santiago and describes how pianists and drummers dropped in to play for food and drink, mostly blues.
246.ch: Bands, halls and the Smoky Mary
246.q: Them were the, well, them piano players. Most any fellas would come up and play piano. You understand? Did they know many pieces, or just a couple of blues? Oh yeah, well there's the blues. They didn't want nothing but the blues. When you play the piano in the supper, they wanted the blues singing…

590.t: Paul Barnes, his mutes, and pianist Lloyd Glenn
590.s: Alcorn talks about trumpeter Paul Barnes, his mutes, and how Barnes left a job and Alcorn stayed on in his place. Alcorn also identifies pianist Lloyd Glenn and recalls recording with him in California.
590.q: Paul Barnes. He was fast on his life, wasn't he? Did you ever play with Paul? No, in later years. So then, just after he started in his Dixieland music, whenever he worked as a big band, never played one job with him in a big band. See, when he went to Petter, the job was getting kind of rough for…

249.t: His wife's piano style and solos
249.s: Her piano style and whether pianists took solos in those days.
249.q: Yeah, she was wonderful on that. I just wondered if they did in those days. Yeah, all the same way they take... Played mostly chords and...

179.s: Joe James could not read but swung a band, stayed with Thomas until he died; Thomas now has Charlie Hamilton.
179.q: Yeah, he died too. I don't know who Thomas got playing piano with him now but that's how he stayed with Thomas until he died, Joe James did.

253.t: Sugar Underwood and Florida blues pianists
253.s: Allen asks about blues pianists around Savannah and Jacksonville, notably Sugar Underwood, who played in all the black keys.
253.q: that guy. And he was a good piano player too. Very good. Yeah, I heard the record, somebody played a record of him.

180.t: Clarence Todd and Camilla Todd, pianists in the Pelican band
180.s: Clarence Todd, his sister Camilla and Clarence Williams recordings come up in discussion.
180.q: Clarence Todd, they got Clarence Williams and they got Clarence Todd.

172.s: Allen and Ridgley sort out Emanuel Perez and Manuel Manetta, whom Ridgley calls a fine piano player and teacher.
172.q: Menela. That's who I want them to speak them. And he was a fine fellow, a fine piano player. For them he didn't do nothin' but teach them them.

250.t: Piano styles, Dizzy Norman and the old pianist Boisot
250.s: Bergen prefers a piano player who keeps rhythm; recalls Earl Hines imitator Dizzy Norman and the old-time pianist Boisot, whose tapes he kept.
250.q: Boisau's style, when I was coming up I didn't go for it because everything was Father Hines when I was coming up. And if you didn't play like Father Hines, the closest thing to Father Hines was a fellow I played with by the name of Dizzy Norman. Later on he was with Bois Maesick. He was not with…

32.t: Blind Boone, Charleston music teachers and church music
32.s: White names Blind Boone and the Charleston teachers who trained him, and describes the city's churches, organs and choirs.
32.q: What are you going to do about Blind Boone and Scott Joplin? What are you going to do about it? Now, Blind Boone did not read any music, but he had a teacher when he was a little boy. He did have his sight and he read Blind before he- He came from Missouri somewhere.

430.t: Dude Amaker and piano in the district
430.s: The interviewer asks about pianist Frank 'Dude' Amaker, who worked in the district.
430.q: Did he work around with him? No, he worked in the district, yeah. He worked at Pete Lawlinson, all the places now. Red Light District.

34.t: Barrelhouse pianists he knew in New Orleans
34.s: After a remark about Little Brother Montgomery, he names Jelly Roll Morton, Walter Pichon and Joe Robichaux as pianists he knew.
34.q: read jerry jerry robert martin i knew him oh yeah and i knew uh walter p sean oh he could that's he could read music though yeah and i knew uh joe dragas joe robichaud joe robichaud uh dear to play in the nightclubs down there. 770.s: Teagarden describes Kelley's self-teaching, practice, classical influences and how overwhelming his playing was.
770.q: Well, he's self-taught, but he used to listen to, uh, everybody that came through Houston. Especially, there used to be quite a few colored boys that come through Houston, you know, from New Orleans. Yeah. And there was quite, quite a lot of, uh, entertainment in that city at that time. And, uh, I…

254.s: Allen asks about two pianists playing against each other; they mention the rough Butcher's Hill spot by the levee.
254.ch: Reel 2: race, storm and Bolden vs Robichaux
254.q: Two people playing against one another. You know, I never knew I was there. I never knew I was there. I never knew I was there. Did you ever go to Butcher Hills? Butcher Hills, yeah, sure. That's right there. The oak and the levee there.

771.s: Steve Lewis traveled with Billy Mack's show before joining Bocage's band, was self-taught, could not read but had a wonderful ear.
771.q: Well Steve, he used to go on, he traveled with a show called Billy Mack, you know. And we had another boy playing with us called Arthur Campbell. Well Arthur left me, he went to Chicago, see. Well Steve came in town and he come out and started playing with us. Well in Carroll family. Yeah, he…

772.t: Favorite pianists: Fats Pichon, Steve Lewis, Earl Hines, Fats Waller
772.s: He names the pianists he liked, including Fats Pichon, Steve Lewis, Hines and Waller, who set the styles others followed.
772.q: Oh yeah, well, his piano player that I liked around in New Orleans was Fats Pichon. I liked his playing until he was down there, worked with us down there by the Absinthe House. I was down there. I mean, after he went blind in there, I think that's about the best piano player I would've got. Well,…

241.t: Hunting for a pianist's name and a four-piece dance band
241.s: They try to recall a red-haired pianist and discuss a four-piece band in a big dance hall.
241.ch: Weddings and playing for private parties
241.q: Really Gallo. Yeah. He played something there. He tried to, you know, he had to play piano for a good while. So he was trying to, you know, play the old kid. Yeah. He was trying to play the piano. He was trying to play the piano. He's gone in and I don't want to go here and if I can't try to do…

773.t: The Cadillac nightclub band: Adolph Ducanger and the pianist George
773.s: Her husband's Olympia band at the Cadillac; piano players Adolph Ducanger and a George who went to Chicago are discussed, with the interviewer trying to place him.
773.ch: Arnold DePass's life and the Cadillac years
773.q: That was Arnold's band. You know, that was the Olympia band. And then he had Adolph Ducanger. He got killed, you know. You heard of him. Yes, well, I've heard of him.

577.t: The Clam House, Monk and leaving New Orleans at nineteen
577.s: He recalls the Clam House after-hours piano scene and talks about the ten years away, 1926 to 1936.
577.q: Yeah, I knew Pop. I knew Fats Duarte was pretty good. We used to go up to the hall and after hours and time, you know, I'll tell you about that place called the Clam House. They had a big colored piano playing piano and all the piano players used to come up and sit and play. Like Willie the Lion…

262.s: Allen asks about pianist Camilla Todd and Celestin's women piano players.
262.q: with Celestine. Celestine? I remember the head of a woman who used to play with him. I remember with him. But I never did know her name, you know? She was a pretty nice piano player. Oh, he's had good piano players. Yeah. Probably it could be the same

774.t: Other pianists she heard and being chaperoned
774.s: She recalls pianist Walter Decou, and says she was always chaperoned by her uncle, brothers and sons.
774.q: That's why I always had someone with me. Yes. See, when I left my uncle, I went with my brothers, and they were with my sons.

37.t: Dixieland pianists in Chicago and the New Orleans piano tradition
37.s: They criticise Chicago pianists shaped by modern habits, and discuss whether New Orleans produced any piano school beyond Jelly Roll Morton and Tony Jackson.
37.q: here on Chicago by and large it seems to me have been influenced very much during the past ten years by the modern characteristics of playing and I I suspect that there are a great many crutches that these guys use a little locked hand chords and and and rhythmic patterns that seem to me to be very…

265.t: Gang Kid and the pianist Thomas
265.s: Wilson knows Gang Kid and recalls Thomas, a blues pianist at parties.
265.q: Yes I know him. Drive them down. Drive them down. And we had a fellow, he used to play around parties, and the deals around that. We used to call him, his name was Thomas. In other words he was a ballast music player, we had ballast music, but that's what the people wanted in my day. Oh yeah. They…

38.t: Teddy Weatherford and Tate's Theater Band
38.s: Levy rates Teddy Weatherford among the tops and they discuss his India recordings and Tate's band.
38.q: Yes. Mm-hmm. He didn't have quite the, the improvising technique of Cass. Cass was tremendous. He was really tremendous. And that Teddy Weatherford that you heard, I can speak about, he was, he was among the tops too. It was, but I mean, in those days, it's not like you look back over it, you know.…

126.t: White cabaret pianists in New Orleans, c.1912-14
126.s: He recalls Erwin LeClaire, Leonard Beisdorfer and Joe Virgis playing cabarets; he did not hear Tony Jackson.
126.q: Well, in those days, uh, I think that the boys that we played with will remember Erwin LeClaire. I don't think that Erwin ever really followed his music, as well as, uh, Leonard Beisdorfer and, uh, Joe Virgis. Uh, Joe Virgis had composed some tunes in his day, and he was quite a well-known pianist,…

401.t: Stale Bread, the black-key piano player
401.s: Williams says Stale Bread played the black keys, claimed to have created jazz, and has a grave he visited.
401.q: Well, he used to play Black Keys, you know. Black Keys. Okay, alright. And he claims he wrote the voice, he's a creator of jazz. That out, I got a paper about it, and on his grave he's got something about that. See, his daughter is married to Mr. Weaver. And I was out to the side, Tony came out, or…

775.t: Manuel Perez's pianist in the Oliver band
775.s: Asked about Manuel Moneta, Stevenson thinks he played piano with that band.
775.q: I think he was playing piano. I think he was playing piano. I think he was playing piano.

2.t: Talking with Morton: his records, Simeon and his left hand
2.s: Morton's remembered records under other names, Simeon, flutter tonguing, and his piano style as orchestra.
2.q: He said, here's a man who knows all my pieces and all. He was very pleased. So after talking a while, he said he'd made so many records he couldn't remember all of them. He mentioned, at that time, we didn't know all of his records either and we still probably don't. But he mentioned he'd made some…

21.t: Best piano players of his youth
21.s: He names Tony Jackson, Alfred Wilson and Albert Cal, who played with Robichaux, as the finest pianists.
21.ch: Jelly Roll, Boyman Ham and piano players
21.q: He was from, he was from Miss Lula's home, I think, of White Castle, too. He played piano with John Robichaud.

272.t: Blind Gilbert and the blind pianist Blind Jack
272.s: The interviewer asks about blind trumpeter Gilbert; Lizana describes Blind Jack, who took spot jobs and travelled the city alone.
272.q: Now we had another thing that you won't find very often. We had a piano player. We call him Blind Jack. He's blind. Jack, he didn't play with a steady, but pick him up on jobs every night and things like that. Spot jobs. He's the only man that's ever been known to do it when he's going to tell you.…

275.s: He tells of walking into a club where Hoagy Carmichael was casually playing piano.
275.q: Oh, yeah. Hoagie Carmichael. He is from Terre Haute, Indiana. It's his home. And I was appearing at one of the nightclubs there. And a funny incident happened. And after we finished our show, we went over to the club where he happened to be in. He wasn't playing there, but he was in there. And we…

43.t: Piano players she worked with and Charlie Taylor's orchestra
43.s: She lists the many pianists she worked with, names Fats Waller and Willie Smith as favorites, and praises Charlie Taylor's orchestra, which she most enjoyed singing with.
43.q: Fat Waller, Fat Waller, Willie Smith, the Lion, oh, like I told you, Leroy Smith, I can't think of what his name, Brooks, Brooks, Porter Granger, Jelly Roll Martin, Clarence Johnson, Donald Haywood, Donald Haywood, Russell Robison, Clarence Williams, Clarence Williams, Glover Compton, Hutchinson,…

45.t: Piano players around New Orleans and Buddy Christian
45.s: Williams names pianists he knew or knew of, including Steve Lewis, Tony Jackson, Udell Wilson, Arthur Campbell and Buddy Christian.
45.ch: Opening talk: pianists and Buddy Petit
45.q: Oh, I was a man. You know Udell Wilson. Oh, Udell, yes, indeed. Who wouldn't know Udell? Yes, indeed. Yeah, Udell. And this other piano player, I'm trying to think of his name, he went to Chicago, never come back. New York, at least.

664.t: What a lead or take-off piano player does
664.s: Brownlee was a lead piano who set the tempo and key, played the intro, then played chords.
664.q: Play the introduction and the number, you know. And bring you right into the key you're going in and set the tempo for you. And then the trumpet man would take you from there.

482.t: Poor Ray Nolan, Jimmy Cato and other pianists he knew
482.s: Asked about more pianists, Tuts recalls Poor Ray Nolan, Jimmy Cato and his cousin Adam Cato, and little Butch.
482.q: Do you know a piano player named Ford? No. Or Poor Ray Nolan? Poor Ray, uh, I knew Poor Ray, he was an old man too when I was a kid. A bright fella, he died and he doesn't go too. But I never knew too much about him. Yeah, what do you mean by years ago? After the World War? Yeah, yeah, he's been…

121.t: Pianos in the house and cousin Joe Mitchell versus Toots Washington
121.s: Houses had pianos; uncle Robert Wilson played, and cousin Joe Mitchell claimed to outplay Toots Washington before going to sea.
121.q: What high it was, the houses that had pianos in them. See, most houses, any way people that had any kind of little money, they would all have a piano in the house. Mm-hmm. And, uh, my uncle, uh, Robert Wilson, he's a minister, he used to, he was one of these piano players like Professor Longhead.…

190.t: A pianist who played chords by ear, and a saxophonist felled by strokes
190.s: Purnell describes a piano player who could not read but played all the chords and sang well, and the speakers recall a saxophone player who had two strokes.
190.q: That was the one that learned my brother. Yeah. He put some. I said, see man, when did you start playing piano? Boy was some surprise. That boy says, man, look at this boy. Oh man, I can play. He can't play nothing. Boy come. One time we stopped for a piano player. The piano player got sick of it.…

776.t: Burroughs Lovingood and the twin pianos with Fate Marable
776.s: Verne recalls pianist Lovingood, now in Washington, and the twin pianos with Fate Marable.
776.ch: St. Louis bands and other players
776.q: He wants to come down here and play the clap before us, or play, uh, right now on the board. He lives in Washington, D.C. And I heard from the other day. Called him over long distance phone. And, uh, yes.

777.s: Allen asks about pianist Mamie Desdune; Williams knows a Desdune relative and will ask.
777.q: I like him. He lived up here. He used to be a piano player himself but he don't play anymore. He's been all up the country playing. I ask the daddy to me. I do.

778.t: Willie Woods, a schoolmate pianist who needed sheet music
778.s: Willie Woods played only from copies, later became an x-ray technician in Detroit and never played in bands.
778.q: She just, you know, she'd come to my house and sit down and try to play piano with me, but she always wanted me to play. Because I always had a piano there in Detroit. Did she ever play with bands, do you know? No, I ain't never really played with no bands. Even in Pensacola she played in a band.

648.t: Barrelhouse music and slow drags explained
648.s: Barrelhouse is slow bluesy piano with small groups; chatter about a visitor arriving.
648.ch: Origins of jazz and the district
648.q: Oh, Barrel House, that's kind of hard to explain. It's a type of piano... All slow, more of the blues type, you know? And... Everything was dragged out. It was dragged out more or less in those days. And in fact, none of them had any what you'd call Dixieland combinations. Some of the places could…

779.t: Raymond Burke and pianist Sidney Wilson
779.s: Brief work with Raymond Burke, and pianist Sidney Wilson at the Palace Theatre.
779.ch: Stories of players and the sister
779.q: Sidney Wilson was one of the finest piano players I've ever played. He played in the Palace Theatre. For years he was great. Very good friend of mine too, for many years. He used to come out and see us, and of course he's living, I believe, last we heard he was supposed to be living in Baton Rouge.…

649.t: Memphis piano players: Florida Street Snooki and Big Maceo

He was actually about the only song he was singing, but he played all poplar and blues. Yeah. What was his name? And late at night, he was one of them. He called…

288.t: Willie Jackson singing at Tom Anderson's; Piron's band
288.s: Tom Anderson hired his own singer, identified as Willie Jackson; Charles remarks on Piron's weak piano player and New York records.
288.ch: Society work, Camilla Todd and Storyville
288.q: No, we didn't have, we didn't sing no blues. Well we played the blues but we didn't sing. You didn't sing, not those words. When we were playing at Tom Anderson though, we used to have a special fellow there, especially to sing. And every now and then he'd sing a song or two.

642.t: Wilhelmina Barth, pianist on the jitney dance
642.s: He describes Barth's piano style, size and touch, and what he knows of her later life.
642.q: Well, like I told you, Bill, on a Jitney dance, you see the styles varied. When she came to work early at night, she might have played like pad of whiskey, like you say. But as the hours started to go, she was finally wide up playing like stormy weather, you know, just sitting up there caught in…

572.t: Johnny Miller's piano and Chick Martin
572.s: He describes New Orleans piano players in Dixieland bands and his friendship with Chick Martin.

And, uh, he's the guy that, that, that was on, on, I thought, a trip around, uh, when we first started, started the band when I joined Johnny,…

193.t: Billie Pierce: Pensacola, her wedding, bands and blues singers
193.s: Billie Pierce talks about growing up in Pensacola, meeting De De, her wedding, New Orleans clubs and bandleaders, and playing with blues singers like Bessie Smith and Ida Cox.

289.t: Dispute over whether Ray Charles played on Slim's session
289.s: The interviewer says Ray played piano on Things I Used to Do; Stovall, who was at the session, disputes it.
289.q: Yeah, well during that time, when he actually got big then, he was with Rip Robert then. You know, Rip was the biggest type then.

290.t: Sam Dutrey Sr., Arthur Williams and Camilla Todd
290.s: Sam Dutrey Sr. played with LaCaze often; Arthur Williams was a clarinetist; Camilla Todd a pianist he worked with.

290.q: Sam Dutry Sr., he played with me quite a bit. You know, we was practically in the same age group. And we were pretty good friends. And he played with me quite a bit. He never was a member of the band. He played with us quite a bit.

602.t: Pernell's piano and the Rene rhythm section
602.s: Gabriel discusses Alton Purnell's piano style in Rene's band and how Tisdale, Rene and he covered the rhythm.
602.q: And Houston, William Houston came into Rene's band after that. And then he was also in Sidney Desvinge's band when I played with him.

52.t: Steve Lewis and Walter Pichon, piano styles
52.s: After a garbled exchange about Richard Jones, Mason discusses pianists Steve Lewis and Walter Pichon and their ragtime and cocktail styles.
52.q: I know Steve, yes, Steve Lewis. Did you like his playing? Well of course he played a style that was quite popular at that time when I heard it. You see they had ragtime piano plays at that time and this music like Swinging Down the Lane and those tunes of course, they were not so popular around…

690.t: Piano in dance bands and Edward Wright
690.s: Pope's bands always had piano; his pianist Edward Wright became an arranger in Chicago.
690.q: Well we played with the piano most of the time. Always had a piano playing. In fact, I had one of the best piano players I believe... well... I don't know what he... he composed some music and he was an arranger for some concern in Chicago.

644.s: Lala recalls Joe Garrow the pianist who played Bucktown with Dan Tagnett and a drummer.
644.q: No. This boy, he wouldn't put an extra noise, he'd ruin the tune. What do you know? He wouldn't put an extra noise, he'd ruin the tune. I know. He wouldn't put an extra noise. He wouldn't put an extra noise. This played a chord. Well, I know he's a bar. I wouldn't play a Joe Garrow. I know. No, no.…

84.t: Steve Lewis the pianist and singer
84.s: Steve Lewis, piano player and singer of smutty songs, drawing crowds and money and drinking, and Handy's remark on Piron's difficult music.
84.ch: New Orleans clarinetists and Steve Lewis
84.q: Oh, Steve Lewis is a wonderful piano player. Likes to crack a lot of jokes, and he sing a lot of songs with a lot of smutty things to it.

780.t: Other New Orleans pianists of the fifties
780.s: He recalls a pianist playing Caravan, Paul Gayten and Salvador Doucette.
780.ch: Piano, Guitar Slim and personal life
780.q: No. No, no. No, no, no. No, no. No, no. Oh, God dog, what's his name? No. No, no. I remember him. I remember him. I remember him. The first time I heard him play, I heard him play Caravan. And I really, I really, I really, uh, blocked his style. Um, Santee, I think his name was Santee. I think his…

573.t: No piano on the records; May and the club on Rampart
573.s: They used no piano on records, but used a woman called May when sight-reading was needed.
573.q: Yes, between Aberville and Bienville. Oh, yeah. Yeah, that's where the athletic club is. That's the place. That's the place.

781.t: Steve Lewis, Willie Jackson records and Freddie Keppard
781.s: Allen mentions Willie Jackson's records with Steve Lewis; Murray says Steve Lewis played piano with Freddie Keppard and Piron.
781.q: Oh Steve Lewis, yeah he used to play piano. He played piano right there. Well Steve Lewis played piano with, what is this man's name? Fredy Kaplan.

782.s: He explains his own piano influences and names Jimmy Yancey as his favorite; both men praise Yancey's simplicity.
782.q: Well, I guess, what it most sounds like is probably like Elton Bonner. But it's not that he's my favorite piano player. It's just that I think it fits in good with the band I play. And it's simply, I think it's the style that I can come closer to. True, I don't have the good technique. And he don't…

298.t: Albert Walters on piano; doubling on piano
298.s: Met Albert Walters at a West End club with Paul Moore; talk of horn men who double on piano.
298.ch: Billy and De De Pierce, Al Hirt tour
298.q: Yeah, I worked with him. Him and I were working in that club back in West End. Used to have nightclubs in West End? With the same Paul Moore. I'll tell you what. Albert was. That's where I first met Albert. He was on piano and I was on band. He worked with Paul Moore, his band back then. Back then.…

177.t: Piano and drum house parties and Frazier pianists
177.s: Piano and drum jobs at lawn parties were plentiful; Jiles worked with Mitchell and Simon Frazier and a pianist called Herman.
177.q: Oh they had lots of piano and drums, because they had a lot of house parties, what they would call lawn parties. That was practically, they had more jobs than the bands did, piano and drums.

783.t: Ragtime players of St. Louis: Joplin, Turpin, Joe Jordan
783.s: The interviewer asks about ragtime; Shoffner recalls Scott Joplin and Tom Turpin, knew Joe Jordan from Chicago, and cannot recall an old ragtime pianist in East St. Louis.
783.q: Yeah, there's Patterson. There's another piano player over there now, you know old-time one. He lives in East St. Louis now. Oh, I can't recall this name.

476.t: Desdunes band trumpet, trombone and pianist Warren Bennett
476.s: One trumpet (George McCollum), Raymond Brown on trombone, and Warren Bennett, a fast pianist and reed player from Bay St. Louis.
476.q: He had lightning fingers. He played piano, you know, he played piano like it, those Buenos Aires. That's right. The closest to Buenos Aires I know. Uh-hmm. He had, he had, he had, he was just as fast on a clarinet of saxophone too. Didn't they have a contest between them two at the Pelican? I…

128.t: Piano players: May, Tink and Emma
128.s: No piano on the record; Robinson talks about pianists May, Tink and Emma who worked with Papa Celestin after the Tuxedo split.
128.q: I didn't use a woman called, a lady called May Now her last name I don't know about She was a good piano player, she was a good musician, May She was a good piano player

307.s: Thomas identifies pianist Jeanette Kimball and her ex-husband Norvin, and says Celestin took Jeanette into the band as a girl, so they should be interviewed.
307.q: Norvin. Norvin. N-E-R-V-I-N. He's the one that used to play band. That's Jeanette's former. Yeah, ex-husband or something. Yeah, ex-husband. Jeanette's still with the band. Jeanette Kimball, yeah, she's still with the band. We haven't interviewed her yet, or him.

3.t: Chicago pianists: Clarence Jones, Dave Payton, Teddy Weatherford, Earl Hines
3.s: They discuss other Chicago pianists and where they worked.
3.q: Very good, but he wasn't the musician. You see, Dave Payton worked at the Grand Theatre for Gibbs, and then he worked at the Regal.

155.s: Budd on Confrey's tunes like Kitten on the Keys, their awkward keys, and Dick Hyman's playing of them.
155.q: You can only play it — that’s another thing about — Zezz Confrey is one that I got interested in the early days. I heard him on records and of course the hit “Song Out Of Songs.” They called that novelty piano playing in those days. And his big hit was “Kitten on the Keys.” And everybody to this…

320.t: Hines's reputation and style; bringing back Helen Humes
320.s: Dance says Hines's 1928 fame made him seem old-fashioned though he revolutionized piano, and recommends Teddy Wilson's book. Dance also recalls persuading Helen Humes to return for a Basie revival at Carnegie Hall.
320.q: Well you see that actually worked against him. Because here’s a man who made his name really in 1928. He made “Weather Bird” with Louis and “West End Blues” which are two of the most famous records in jazz history. So people think, would automatically think of him as being old fashioned, because he…

466.s: He names Jimmy Rowles, Mel Powell, Teddy Wilson, Nat Cole, Tatum and especially Erroll Garner.
466.q: Yeah I do. The first thing that comes into my mind is Jimmy Rowles. I’ve always been crazy about his playing, ever since I heard the records he made in the 1940s, I was crazy about his playing. And when I finally met him years later, he didn’t disappoint me. He was just — he’d even become a greater…

616.t: Dream band pianists: Bill Charlap, Ted Rosenthal, Bill Mays
616.s: He names Bill Charlap first, talks about liking the people you play with, and names Rosenthal and Mays.
616.q: Number one is the guy I play with Phil Woods, Bill Charlap. He’s not really like famous like a lot of other piano players although I expect he will be some day, but he’s just a wonderful, wonderful pianist. I don’t know how to describe it, he’s brought up — his father was Moose Charlap, who wrote…

332.t: Horace Silver, Monk, Art Tatum and virtuosity
332.s: Ingham admires Horace Silver, Blakey, Monk and especially Art Tatum's harmonic mind, comparing Tatum to Liszt.
332.q: It was great. I loved it too. Yeah, you’re right. Yeah that’s where I like the Horace Silver band, when I was lucky enough to hear Horace in London. I mean that kind of grease and funk to it. I loved Horace Silver. That came out of bebop, but it had that wonderful quality. Blakey too.

695.t: Teenage favorites: big bands and Earl Hines
695.s: As an organist she favored McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Henderson, Millinder and Ellington, and credits Earl Hines with making the left hand important and playing tenths.
695.q: Well first of all you see I played organ. By this time I was accomplished somewhat on the organ. And so I looked at everything from an orchestral point of view. And my favorite bands at that time, when I was a teenager, were the McKinney Cotton Pickers, Fletcher Henderson, Lucky Millinder and then…

334.t: Hank Jones and respect for great musicians
334.s: He heard Hank Jones with Goodman, and expresses respect for Jones, Wilson, Hines and Young.
334.q: When I heard Hank Jones the very first time, Hank played with the Benny Goodman Orchestra, Hank Jones. And he played very good. Oh he’s the best pianist. But I met Hank Jones. Hank says, “Teddy Wilson is the best pianist.” Hank says. But everybody says great musicians, best musician, best musician.…

581.t: Recording live at the Vanguard with Earl Hines
581.s: Playing with Earl Hines, Budd Johnson and Gene Ramey without rehearsal, and Hines's ring flying off.
581.ch: Playing, learning and the music's values
581.q: Oh that was something. That “Live at the Vanguard.” That’s one of my favorite things that I made. It was almost the same kind of thing. He was the nicest man. The nicest guy. I mean whooh. He was the nicest person, oh man. And we never rehearsed. I never rehearsed with him either. It was Budd…

784.t: Kenny Drew and Tommy Flanagan: following without rehearsal
784.s: He contrasts tricky pianists like Flanagan with Kenny Drew, who gave no instructions on tour and in studio.
784.q: I know Junior’s whole repertoire. As a matter of fact I produced two albums on Junior’s name for my label for the record company. So me and Junior is like, I spoke to Junior the other day, and we did three tours of Japan together. Junior — you have to be special to work with Junior. Junior has a —…

785.t: A YouTube comment on 'Yesterday' and Erroll Garner's influence
785.s: A commenter hears Garner in Sands's left hand; Sands praises Garner's influence on all jazz piano.
785.q: All right. Be easy on me too man. XX: So an unintentional touch of Errol Garner at the start, Christian’s left hand was on the beat, not a fraction behind, as in Garner’s case. Should he have approached this McCartney evergreen. Excellent rendition, Christian, keep on keeping on.

218.t: Losing interest in Tatum; playing for show
218.s: He found Tatum less interesting over time and thinks such playing, like all public work, is for show.
218.q: And there was a lot of scale work and stuff and transpositions and transitions and stuff. But after a while I found him not so interesting as I thought he was.

672.s: She distinguishes accompanists from pianists, naming Don Trenner, Ron Elbright and Lou Mathews, and says it is about listening.
672.q: Yeah. That was unheard of. I mean it was like “I beg your — what did you say?” “I don’t know if I can accompany you as well yet.” And he worked at it. Because it is a different thing, being an accompanist as opposed to playing piano. I’ve had many pianists. Don Trenner was an accompanist as was Ron…

61.t: Erroll Garner, a man who gave no interviews
61.s: Garner was a charming kid from Pittsburgh who couldn't read music; no published interviews exist.
61.ch: Erroll Garner and the long-playing revolution
61.q: Yeah, that’s true. I never realized that until I saw a reference to that, and Martha mentioned it again years later. I didn’t realize that, that there were no interviews published about Erroll. As a matter of fact, I never knew that much about Erroll until the book by James Doran came out, which…

526.t: Playing piano and organ on A Genuine Tong Funeral
526.s: Shown the personnel, she says she played composer's piano and organ and other parts as needed but was not a serious pianist then.
526.ch: Marriages, Tong Funeral and Liberation Music
526.q: It isn’t that that’s incorrect, your information. It’s just that I played piano and organ on that probably and I probably also played chains and glockenspiel and anything else that was necessary.

133.s: Walton knows Hank Jones only minimally, from Japan tours and his dry humor, and describes him rehearsing Carmen McRae's music in a practice room.
133.ch: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
133.q: Yeah, but I knew him still uh, uh, uh, uh minimally. I don't know him that well. I mean, I speak to him when, you know, and we've been on tours together even in Japan where they have ten pianists. Uh, they called it "a hundred golden fingers." And uh, I got to know him uh, a little bit, you know.…

101.s: Hines's trumpet-style piano and Wiggins as an underrated accompanist.
101.q: Earl Hines was a marvelous leader. I didn’t have an opportunity to work too much with Gates, except on a couple of occasions with a small group, after he had Marva [Josie], the singer, and Budd Johnson was with him at the time. But he was a nice man, a great musician. I’m very proud of the fact…

143.s: Herman Foster needed no rehearsals and stole the show from Dave Brubeck in Belgium.
143.q: They never said a thing about Herman, and Herman was a genius. Herman was a guy... Sometimes we’d play a year and never have a rehearsal. He knew everything. He was a genius. We played a concert once in Belgium. The guy had Dave Brubeck on there. I went and told the promoter, “You’d better let us…

86.t: The Stockholm pianist who knew no tunes
86.s: He tells of the Swedish bandleader-pianist who didn't know standards.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: Yeah, I remember that happened in Sweden. That happened in Stockholm. I finally asked him, “Well, do you know ‘Sometimes I’m Happy’?” He says, “Yeah.” Me too. Sometimes I’m happy too. There was a piano player, then after I found out he was the bandleader I stopped kidding him then. He was the…

371.t: Earl Hines and single-line versus two-handed piano
371.s: Jones knew Hines from records and heard him in Flint; Hines's trumpet-style lines foreshadowed bebop, unlike the two-handed Waller and Tatum.
371.q: Well, first of all, through recordings. See, the recordings were really the only means that we had of hearing these big bands because most of them did not come through our area very often. Once in a while they would come, but I heard them many records. I heard Earl on many records. I know he did a…

135.t: John Lewis as an economical accompanist
135.s: Heath describes John Lewis's playing in Dizzy's band, his part on Two Bass Hit, and the early Milt Jackson quartet.
135.q: He was a great accompanist from the moment we heard him. He did something on “Two Bass Hit” behind Ray Brown that everybody was saying, “Listen to John Lewis behind that!” [sings] Some kind of rhythmic thing he set up when the band came in after Brown’s solo. John Lewis has always been a phenomenal…

451.q: Yeah. I think Mary Ann Topper was managing Michel as well as me, and she put it together. I’m trying to remember if I had ever heard him play at all but… As you know, he had… I don’t know the technical term, but it was glass bone disease. He had no calcium. And he got about this high. I don’t think…

471.s: Cobb talks about Wynton Kelly's gift, prodigy years, seizures, and Monty Alexander's and Grace Metivier's efforts to keep his memory alive.
471.q: That only happened when he got to be a grown man. That didn’t happen through the first part of his life. I don’t know what that was that happened. He got – I think he claimed that happened maybe after Paul died, that he was – he liked Paul so much, he started – he used to drink a lot. He was in a…

165.t: Nat Cole as a jazz pianist
165.s: Hendricks praises Nat Cole as a top jazz pianist he met through Art Tatum.
165.q: He was one of the ten best jazz pianists. He could play. I met him, because I was working in Toledo with Art, and he’d come to see Art. That’s how we met. But he was a great jazz musician, very hip.

589.t: Earl Hines and the pianists his father played
589.s: His father introduced him to Hines, Tatum and Teddy Wilson; Lewis explains Hines' role leaving stride and recalls two dinners with him.
589.q: Earl “Fatha” Hines was in my life because of my dad. Earl “Fatha” Hines, Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson – my dad brought all that into my life, and that’s how – that’s also the Nat “King” Cole. If you go – if you follow Nat back as a piano player, you get into Teddy Wilson, you get into Earl “Fatha”…

492.t: Phineas Newborn's genius and the seed he planted
492.s: Lloyd describes listening to Phineas play through a screen door and says Phineas planted the seed for his piano-player collaborations.
492.ch: Phineas Newborn and the Memphis blues circuit
492.q: Not only that, he never caviled. He had no negativity, he was a positive soul. Very sweet, very self-effacing. But he could sit at that piano, and that was a sheer genius. I would ride my little bicycle over, cause he lived - he went to Booker Washington, I lived over on Boyd. I lived near them.…

229.s: Blakeney recalls pianist Gene Wright, the lack of Black residents in Honolulu, the posters row, and a tour of the other islands.
229.q: That was a very interesting job; I can remember Gene Wright, he was one of the better piano players in Los Angeles at that time, but he wasn't very popular. He liked to play classics, he liked to run liked a man who all over the piano. But we/played rhythm, you know, backed us up on our horns, and…

230.t: Turk Van Lake and the Peck Kelly story
230.s: Guitarist Turk Van Lake would not leave New York, which Barnet compares to Houston pianist Peck Kelly.
230.ch: Singers, Las Vegas, Hodges and road life
230.q: Well, he was a fabulous piano player that lived back in the '20s, and he lived in Houston, Texas, and people would come from all over the country. He was just a fabulous piano player. And the old story was yeah, but you can't get him to leave town. He had offers from Paul Whiteman, no, he wouldn't…

113.t: Tatum needed no drummer and loved to play and sing the blues
113.s: He says Tatum needed no rhythm section and could throw drummers off, and that Tatum loved the blues and sometimes sang them.
113.ch: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
113.q: It didn't bother him at all. It might bother the drummer. The drummer or whoever else is there, because he did so many things, you know what I mean. It just -- that just made the drummer out of concept with what was happening. Basie or whoever else was sitting in there, the whole thing was out of…

26.t: Seminole, the raggedy pianist-xylophonist at the Capitol Palace
26.s: Greer recalls a young pianist from Jersey who out-played Willie the Lion and others.
26.q: '22. Capital Palace. It was a hangout for everybody in Harlem. So we Willie there and Lionel (?) had a band, Charlie Irvis was playing with him. Anyway, we'd hang out there. It was a hangout, me and Duke was hanging out together. We went down there and Duke -- they loved Duke.

17.ch: Big bands, small groups and studio work
17.q: : Oh Teddy, Teddy is just great. See I'll never forget when Teddy first came to New York is when I was first with Benny Carter. Benny sent for him, Teddy Wislon, and Keg Johnson, is where they joined. And I thought then, I used to love Earl Hines piano playing, but Teddy was just a step ahead of…

67.t: Pianist George Hall and the two great Chicago pianists
67.s: He remembers George Hall but says Teddy Weatherford and Earl Hines were the only great pianists in Chicago.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Well, I guess so. I guess he was a good pianist. He was all right. In those days there was only two great pianists in Chicago at that time and that was Teddy

106.t: Pianola, Mr. Marshall's ragtime and Lucky Roberts
106.s: The ragtime he heard was mostly on the pianola and Marshall's dance-school playing; he knew of the fine pianist Lucky Roberts.
106.ch: New York, church bands and early training
106.q: Mr. Marshall was also a pianist, but he was not what you would call a "ragtime piano player." He played ragtime but it was for the dance schools and everything. I'm trying to think -- yes, I did know and did hear one wonderful piano player. His name was Lucky Roberts.

146.s: Ben Webster, Tab Smith and Lester all played piano, Lester in flat keys; Charlie Parker never did.
146.q: Yeah. All them cats used to play piano. Now, Charlie Parker is the only I ever know that wouldn't fool no piano. I never did know him to bother with no piano, fool with no piano.

409.s: Dance and Cootie recall Kenny Kersey, a boogie-woogie pianist, who went with Andy Kirk.
409.q: Yeah. He went with Andy Kirk. Andy Kirk Craig took him as a piano player.

452.t: Hiring pianist Boo Pleasant from San Antonio
452.s: Cobb tells how he heard Boo Pleasant play in San Antonio, auditioned her in Houston, and brought her to Chicago where she stayed two years and drew men to the club.
452.ch: Back in Houston, Club Ebony and Boo Pleasant
452.q: Well, I brought her out of San Antonio, Texas. She joined me in -- I heard her in San Antonio at the Lakewood Country Club there, Johnny Phillips' place there. And she and Cecil Scott, the saxophone player that used to be with Bill Doggett that played 'Honky Tonk.'

147.t: Sy Oliver, Willie Smith and Wilcox on the team and gigs
147.s: Crawford says Sy was too delicate for sports, and describes Wilcox's piano playing and the band's gigs.
147.ch: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
147.q: Willie played, good shortstop, Wilcox, [his name was.] You know, he was a lefthanded piano player. I don't see how he got that speed and drive, but up here -- trebles, right hand, but he was actually a left handed piano player.

641.s: Joe remembers Buster Wilson from Mississippi as a gentleman and friend who played like Jelly Roll.
641.ch: Joe Liggins and back to Kid Ory
641.q: Buster originally was from Mississippi, I believe. What I learned is that Buster developed... Him and Jelly Roll used to live together at one time, and they was very good friends -- and Buster played a lot like Jelly. Buster drank, drank a lot of liquor. That's probably what helped put him away,…

117.t: Pianists and clarinetists who influenced him: Lucky Roberts, James P., Fats, Earl Hines
117.s: Freeman names Lucky Roberts, James P. Johnson, Fats Waller and Earl Hines, recalls meeting Roberts at the Life photo and touring with Hines in Britain.
117.q: Yes. But to get back to Hawkins now, I could easily say that I was influenced by Hawkins, but not as strongly as I was by the black singers, the dancers and all the -- especially pianists, I was very much influenced by Lucky Roberts, the great black pianist, James P. Johnson, Fats Waller, Earl…

71.t: Teddy Weatherford compared with Earl Hines and Fats Waller
71.s: Clayton and Dance rate pianist Weatherford against Earl Hines and Fats Waller, and note his best days were in the early twenties.
71.ch: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
71.q: Yes. And he would play with us but when we played a specialty like 'Rhapsody in Blue', you see Teddy was working three or four clubs in one night. He'd play 45 minutes here. Leave here and go across town, 45 minutes there. Leave there and go another place. And he was playing four clubs twice a…

148.t: His own jazz piano and who he listened to
148.s: He calls himself a below-average jazz pianist, describes the 'oompa' style and listening to Wilson, Stacy, Waller and Tatum, and bands rather than writers.
148.q: It charged me up a great deal. I wanted to, but it was too tough to break in. I was still a little too young, I wasn't all that great as a jazz pianist. I never thought I'd been all that great as a jazz pianist.

412.t: Willie the Lion Smith at the Back Room
412.s: Willie the Lion Smith plays opposite Hodes, with Barney Bigard teasing about bumping heads. Hodes was in awe of Willie's stride playing and tells of the trumpeter nicknamed Face.
412.ch: Back Room, Solo Art and George Zack (retyped)
412.q: MR. HODES: Almost immediately we got Chippy Hill to come and sing. And then we got Willie Lion Smith. So we had Willie Lion Smith playing opposite me. As Barney Bigard says when he came in there, I like to come in there and see you two guys bumping heads. I never thought I was doing any bumping of…

454.t: Blind Tom and whether Erroll Garner could read
454.s: Memory pianists; Mingus disputes that Garner could not read, citing Garner's brother.
454.ch: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
454.q: Blind Tom, he say he can go to Europe A Symphony for him, and and play his own band (unintelligible) he can sit down and play at home. That's pretty good. I couldn't do that. That's (unintelligible) a whole lot of memory in it.

96.t: Bobby Short as a boy pianist in Rockford
96.s: He recalls the child Bobby Short.
96.q: It doesn't make any difference because Bobby Short was a young kid, twelve years old. And I had a band that was playing at an hotel in Rockford, Illinois was it? One of those small towns out there, not Joliet...

168.t: Tatum as half improviser, half routine
168.s: Tatum's numbers were about three-quarters set routine and one-quarter improvisation, so Stewart could predict much of what he played.
168.ch: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
168.q: Well, I think you might say he was half and half, improviser and routine, because we had quite a few, the numbers that we played, that we really stuck to the routine of the number. Of course, during the number there was a whole lot of improvisation going on. But the routine was -- three quarters,…

611.t: Skinny Johnson, the Johnson brothers and Joe Steele's arranging
611.s: Waters calls Skinny Johnson one of the greatest pianists he ever heard, names the Johnson brothers, and says Steele's arrangements were crowded, unlike Sy Oliver's, a contrast he links to Wilcox.
611.q: It's only one job that I can remember that I could take courses and was on a jazz gig, was Skinny Johnson. That was a guy who I'll always say that was actually one of the greatest piano players I ever heard, I mean it's a shame that he wasn't known. He was a -

427.t: Boogie woogie pianists Pete Johnson, Albert Ammons and Meade Lux Lewis
427.s: Asked about his quartet, Turner credits the Boogie Woogie Boys with introducing boogie woogie to the world.
427.ch: Black and Tan and Kansas City nightlife
427.q: Wasn't a quartet. It was a bunch of piano players --Boogie Woogie Boys. These cats played...they introduced boogie woogie

6.t: Stride piano as New York piano; Willie the Lion
6.s: Father's friends played stride piano at the house. Procope names Fats Waller, Willie the Lion and James P. Johnson and says he likes the Lion's delicate style best.
6.ch: Family and growing up in Manhattan
6.q: whole lot of friends of my father's, they'd come in the house and jump right on the piano and start playing the piano, you know. Like what they call stride piano. Stride piano's New York piano.

115.t: His biggest kicks: Louis, Earl Hines, Tatum and Teddy Wilson
115.s: Louis was his biggest kick, then Earl Hines, Art Tatum and Teddy Wilson.
115.q: Earl and later I think it was Teddy Wilson.

124.t: Horace Parlan in June Clark's dancing school band
124.s: McRae remembers pianist Horace Parlan, with a crippled hand, working with him at a dancing school, though the dating is confusing.
124.q: You know where Horace Parlan worked with us at? You wouldn't believe. He worked with me with June Clark back in them days at the dancing school.

125.t: Fats Waller as the great piano genius, with Art Tatum
125.s: Thompson heard Fats Waller on records and calls him and Art Tatum the greatest jazz pianists, praising Waller's loud but beautiful playing.
125.ch: Early listening, piano and adolescent conflict
125.q: So it was that early age that I picked up naturally these jazz sounds, and it was first Fat Waller Whiler who I heard play, and he was -- since I've read later, the story of his life, which I think it's called Handful of Keys.

98.s: Lovie Austin was before his time and later played rehearsals and dance classes for Sammy Dyer.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing
98.q: A little before my time, and then she was a rehearsal piano player around here for -- I think it was Sammy Dyer, one of them.

13.s: Hines sometimes played alone, on a small white piano.
13.q: No, it was on the stand. Well, now, if he did a number in the show that they had a little special white piano, and they used to put it out on the floor.

79.t: Art Tatum, the Hawkins session and humble musicians
79.s: Dance praises the Hawkins, Trummy and Earl session. Thomas defends Art Tatum's playing with other musicians, saying he and Duke were humble and wanted others comfortable.
79.q: No, no, no. Tatum, that's Art all Tatum, you know. But, all Tatum played, his background ... according to the people who were playing with him.
